lecture.title: OS for the AI Era & openEuler Intelligence Architecture
objectives: Define Artificial Intelligence (John McCarthy, 1956) and trace the 5-layer AI hierarchy from OS/Infrastructure to Industry Solutions
Explain the openEuler Intelligence ('AI for OS') architecture, including its two interaction entries (Web entry and Intelligent Shell entry)
Differentiate the 5 core functions of openEuler Intelligence: Intelligent Q&A, AI Application Development Framework, Intelligent Optimization, Intelligent Diagnosis, and Intelligent Container Image
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Evolution of AI and the 5-Layer AI Hierarchy
The term **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** was coined by **John McCarthy in 1956** as the *"science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs."* In the modern computing stack, AI is structured into five hierarchical layers built upon the Operating System:

| Hierarchy Layer | Core Components & Examples |
| :--- | :--- |
| **5. Industry Solution** | Finance, Healthcare, Security, Transportation, Gaming (autonomous driving, smart home, VR/AR, UAVs) |
| **4. Technology** | Perception & Analysis, Understanding & Thinking, Decision-making & Interaction (Speech/Image/Video recognition, NLP, Knowledge Graph) |
| **3. Technical Direction** | Speech processing, Computer vision, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Decision-making systems, Big data/Statistical analysis |
| **2. Algorithm** | Machine learning (ML) and Deep learning (DL) |
| **1. Infrastructure & OS** | **openEuler and other OSs**, Hardware/Computing capability, and Big Data |

---

### 2. openEuler Intelligence Architecture ("AI for OS")
**openEuler Intelligence** integrates Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities and a rich knowledge base of openEuler source code and O&M data into the OS toolchain.
* **Two Interaction Entries (Official Ch.01 Quiz Point):**
  1. **Web Entry:** Easy-to-use browser portal providing openEuler knowledge, community announcements, and O&M solutions via intelligent agents.
  2. **Intelligent Shell Entry:** Allows O&M engineers and developers to interact with openEuler in the terminal using **natural human language** for heuristic tuning and fault diagnosis.
* **Core Backend Components:** Orchestration Engine, Historical Context Management, Agent Framework (Intelligent O&M, Intelligent Optimization, CVE Hotfix services), Document Parsing Engine, and **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** Knowledge Base.

---

### 3. Five Core Functions of openEuler Intelligence
1. **Intelligent Q&A:**
   * **Workflow Scheduling:** Combines multiple agent steps into an inseparable **atomic operation** with user-defined error recovery, real-time data transfer between steps, and proactive clarification of vague user prompts.
   * **Task Recommendation:** Semantic intent recognition and next-step guidance based on user habits.
   * **Enhanced RAG:** Pre-processing query rewriting/routing, fragment vectorization/keyword indexing, and **multi-channel retrieval** (vectorized, keyword, and **Chat2DB** with re-ranking/fusion).
   * **Corpus Governance:** Fragment relationship extraction, fragment derivative construction (digests), and **OCR** for hybrid image-text documents.
2. **AI Application Development Framework:** Provides Multi-channel RAG, document governance (deduplication, sensitive data masking, standardization), and **embedding model fine-tuning** (e.g., **BGE models**).
3. **Intelligent Optimization:** Achieves **heuristic system optimization** by collecting and analyzing performance data via natural language interaction.
4. **Intelligent Diagnosis (3 Agents):**
   * **Inspection Agent:** Checks designated IP addresses and outputs an abnormality list (associated container IDs, abnormal CPU/memory metrics).
   * **Demarcation Agent:** Analyzes a selected abnormality and outputs the **top 3 root cause metrics**.
   * **Detection (Location) Agent:** Performs profiling location on root cause metrics and outputs hotspot stack, system time, and performance metrics.
5. **Intelligent Container Image:** Uses natural language to pull images from Docker Hub across **3 container layers**:
   * **Tier 1 (SDK layer):** Hardware enablement libraries only (e.g., **CUDA**, **CANN**).
   * **Tier 2 (SDKs + training/inference frameworks):** Adds TensorFlow/PyTorch (e.g., `tensorflow2.15.0-cuda12.2.0`, `pytorch2.1.0.a1-cann7.0.RC1`).
   * **Tier 3 (SDKs + frameworks + LLMs):** Encapsulates pre-integrated foundation models (e.g., `llama2-7b`, `chatglm2-13b`).
key_takeaways: openEuler Intelligence supports exactly TWO interaction entries: Web entry and Intelligent shell entry (Ch.01 Quiz Q1).

Intelligent Diagnosis relies on three specialized agents in sequence: Inspection Agent (checks IP/container abnormalities) -> Demarcation Agent (outputs top 3 root cause metrics) -> Detection Agent (profiling location & stack hotspots).
Intelligent Container Images are organized into 3 tiers: (1) SDK layer (CUDA/CANN), (2) SDK + Frameworks (PyTorch/TensorFlow), and (3) SDK + Frameworks + LLMs (llama2-7b, chatglm2-13b).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse the three Intelligent Diagnosis agents! Inspection finds abnormal IPs/containers; Demarcation narrows down to the Top 3 root cause metrics; Detection/Location profiles the stack and hotspots.

EXAM TRAP: In openEuler Intelligence RAG, Corpus Governance specifically includes three techniques: (1) Fragment relationship extraction, (2) Fragment derivative construction, and (3) Optical Character Recognition (OCR).

lecture.title: Linux History, GNU/FSF, Open Source Licenses & openEuler Community
objectives: Trace OS history from Multics (1965) and Unix (1969/1970 by Ken Thompson) to Minix (1987 by Andrew S. Tanenbaum) and Linux (1991 by Linus Torvalds)
Compare the 4 freedoms of the Free Software Foundation (FSF) and major open source licenses (Mulan, GPL, LGPL, BSD)
Distinguish openEuler Innovation releases vs. LTS releases, kernel version numbering, and openEuler community portals
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. From Multics and Unix to GNU/Linux
* **Multics (1965):** Bell Labs, MIT, and GE jointly developed the **Multiplexed Information and Computing Service** time-sharing multitasking system. Bell Labs withdrew in 1969.
* **Unix (1969–1970):** **Ken Thompson** at Bell Labs wrote a lightweight OS to run his game *Space Travel*, named **Unix** (Uniplexed Information and Computing Service). **1970** is defined as the **Unix Epoch**. Commercial Unix derivatives include **IBM AIX**, **HP-UX**, and **Digital Unix**.
* **GNU & FSF (1984):** **Richard Stallman** launched the Free Software Campaign and founded the **Free Software Foundation (FSF)**, creating open-source Unix utilities and the **GPL**. FSF defines **Four Freedoms**:
  1. Freedom to run programs for any purpose.
  2. Freedom to learn and modify the source code.
  3. Freedom to redistribute programs.
  4. Freedom to create derivatives.
* **Minix (1987) & Linux (1991):** Professor **Andrew S. Tanenbaum** (Vrije University, Amsterdam) wrote **Minix** for teaching. On **September 17, 1991**, **Linus Torvalds** released the free Linux OS online; **Linux kernel 1.0** was officially released in **1994**. Because Linux combines the kernel with GNU utilities, its full name is **GNU/Linux** (`Linux distribution = Linux kernel + utility software`).

---

### 2. Comparison of Open Source Licenses
In the openEuler code repository, the **`LICENSES`** directory declares the open source licenses in use (defaulting to **MulanPSL v2** for community projects).

| License | Key Rules & Commercial/Derivative Requirements |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Mulan** | **China's first open source license.** Covers 5 aspects: copyright license, patent license, non-trademark license, distribution restriction, and disclaimer/liability limitation. Grants a permanent, global, free, non-exclusive, irrevocable copyright license. |
| **GPL** | **General Public License.** Strictly contagious ("copyleft"): any software that references a GPL library, modifies GPL code, or derives from GPL code **must also use the GPL** (open source and free of charge, though charging for distribution/support is permitted). |
| **LGPL** | **Lesser GPL.** Designed for class libraries. Allows **commercial software to link to an LGPL library without open-sourcing the commercial code**. However, direct modifications or derivatives of the LGPL library itself must remain LGPL. |
| **BSD** | **Permissive license.** Allows modification and redistribution as open-source or **proprietary/commercial software**, provided 3 conditions are met: (1) retain original BSD license in source distributions, (2) include BSD license/copyright in binary docs, (3) **do not use the original software/author/institution name for marketing**. |

---

### 3. Linux Kernel Numbering & openEuler Releases
* **Linux Kernel Version (`X.Y.Z`, hosted at `kernel.org`):**
  * **1st digit (`X`):** Major release.
  * **2nd digit (`Y`):** In traditional 3-digit numbering, an **even** number indicates a **stable version**, while an **odd** number indicates a **version under development**.
  * **3rd digit (`Z`):** Number of revisions. (Example: openEuler 20.03 LTS uses kernel `4.19.90`).
* **openEuler Release Cadence:**
  * **Innovation Release** (e.g., openEuler 20.09): Released **every half a year (6 months)** for technical innovation.
  * **Long-Term Support (LTS) Release** (e.g., openEuler 20.03 LTS, 22.03 LTS, 24.03 LTS): Stable enterprise release published **every 2 years**.
* **Community Contribution Workflow & Portals:**
  * Workflow: `Join community -> Sign CLA -> Join SIG -> Assign issues -> Prepare dev. env. -> Submit code -> Review code`.
  * Key Portals: Official website (`www.openeuler.org`), Code hosting (`gitee.com/openeuler`), Docs (`docs.openeuler.org`), Forum (`forum.openeuler.org`), Issue tracker (`quickissue.openeuler.org`).
key_takeaways: Mulan is China's first open source license covering 5 aspects (copyright, patent, non-trademark, distribution restriction, disclaimer). openEuler declares its licenses in the LICENSES directory.
LGPL permits commercial software to link to LGPL libraries without open-sourcing the commercial code, whereas GPL requires any software referencing/modifying GPL code to also be GPL.
openEuler Innovation releases are published every 6 months (half a year); openEuler LTS (Long-Term Support) releases are published every 2 years.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse Innovation vs. LTS release cycles! Innovation = every half a year (6 months); LTS = every 2 years.
EXAM TRAP: In the traditional 3-digit Linux kernel version scheme taught in Ch.02 (p.33), an EVEN second digit denotes a stable version, and an ODD second digit denotes a development version.

lecture.title: Installing openEuler OS, Hardware Architectures & Partition Planning
objectives: Identify the 6 processor architectures and 4 application scenarios supported by openEuler
Distinguish manual installation (USB, CD-ROM, Virtual CD-ROM/ISO) vs. batch automated installation using Kickstart
Configure recommended boot/system partitions (/, /boot, /boot/efi, swap) and Software Selection profiles (Minimum, Server, Hypervisor)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Pre-Installation Planning: Architectures, Scenarios & Modes
Before installing openEuler, administrators must match the installation ISO package to both the target **chip architecture** and **application scenario** (packages across different architectures are incompatible):
* **6 Supported Processor Architectures:** **x86**, **Arm (AArch64)**, **SW64**, **RISC-V**, **LoongArch**, and **PowerPC**.
* **4 Application Scenarios:** **Server**, **Cloud Computing**, **Edge Computing**, and **Embedded Systems**.
* **Installation Modes:**
  * **Individual Setup:** USB drives, physical CD-ROMs, or virtual CD-ROM drives (mounting `.iso` image).
  * **Batch Installation:** Automated installation using the **Kickstart** tool, which supports:
    1. **Semi-automatic installation:** Specify the location of the kickstart file; Kickstart configures keyboard, language, and partitions automatically.
    2. **Full automation:** The entire OS installation is automated without manual intervention.

---

### 2. Boot Menu & Recommended System Partitions
When booting from the openEuler 24.03/20.03 LTS ISO:
* **Boot Menu Options:**
  * `Install openEuler 24.03 LTS`: Directly install the system.
  * `Test this media & install openEuler 24.03 LTS`: Check the software package integrity first, then install.
  * `Troubleshooting -->`: Rescue and diagnostic mode.
  * Keybindings: `[Up]`/`[Down]` to select, **`e`** to edit the selected boot item, or **`c`** for a command prompt.
* **Recommended Manual Partitions (`Installation Destination`):**
  In manual partitioning mode, you can configure **common (standard) partitions**, **logical volumes (LVM)**, or **thin-provisioning logical volumes**:

| Partition / Mount Point | Purpose & Sizing Guideline |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`/` (Root partition)** | **Everything in Linux starts from the root partition.** Stores core OS directories. |
| **`/boot`** | Stores kernel and boot loader files required for system booting. |
| **`/boot/efi`** | Boot device and application program started by the **Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI/UEFI)**. |
| **`swap`** | Virtual memory swap partition used to swap dirty data from RAM when memory is insufficient. **Sizing rule:** If physical memory is small, set `swap` to **twice (2×) the memory size**; if memory is large, reduce the swap ratio accordingly. |

---

### 3. Software Selection & Root/User Account Creation
* **3 Software Selection Base Environments (openEuler 24.03 LTS):**
  1. **Minimum installation:** Most software is not installed (default CLI); ideal for learning Linux architecture or minimal footprint servers.
  2. **Server:** Installs software packages tailored for enterprise server scenarios.
  3. **Hypervisor:** Installs virtualization host software packages.
* **Root Password & User Creation:**
  * `root` is the super administrator with the highest permissions.
  * **Official Ch.02 Quiz Q1 Note:** Page 45 states *"During openEuler installation, you need to set the password of the root user. You can create a common user as required."* However, **Official Ch.02 Quiz Q1 (p.52)** states: *"(True or false) You do not need to specify the password of the root user during the openEuler OS installation. However, you must specify the password of the root user when logging in to the OS after the installation."* -> **Official Answer Key: A (True)**. Remember this exact wording if it appears verbatim on the exam!
key_takeaways: openEuler supports 6 processor architectures: x86, Arm, SW64, RISC-V, LoongArch, and PowerPC, across 4 scenarios: Server, Cloud, Edge, and Embedded.
For batch automated installations, openEuler uses the Kickstart tool (semi-automatic or full automation).
Recommended partitions are /, /boot, /boot/efi, and swap (set swap to 2x RAM when memory is small); software selection offers Minimum installation, Server, and Hypervisor.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Official Ch.02 Quiz Q1 Verbatim Key): In the official Ch.02 Quiz (p.52), the statement 'You do not need to specify the password of the root user during the openEuler OS installation. However, you must specify the password of the root user when logging in to the OS after the installation' is keyed as A (True). Memorize this exact official answer key!
EXAM TRAP: At the GRUB installation menu, pressing 'e' edits the selected boot item, while pressing 'c' opens a command prompt.

lecture.title: Logging In, CLI vs. GUI Desktops, Virtual Consoles & Bash Shortcuts
objectives: Compare CLI vs. GUI and identify the 5 optional desktop environments supported on openEuler (GNOME, UKUI, DDE, Kiran, XFCE)
Perform local virtual console switching (Ctrl+Alt+F1..F6 / Alt+F1..F6) and remote SSH login (PuTTY, Xshell)
Master shell prompts (# vs. $), user switching (su - username, id), and Bash keyboard shortcuts (Tab, history, Ctrl+A/E/C/L)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. CLI vs. GUI and Optional Desktop Environments on openEuler
* **CLI (Command Line Interface):** Text-based UI driven by keyboard commands, options, and arguments; low resource overhead, scriptable, and the **default interface** after openEuler installation.
* **GUI (Graphical User Interface):** Visual UI driven by mouse interactions (buttons, menus, dialogs) for ease of use. While openEuler installs in CLI mode by default, users can optionally install **five desktop environments**:
  1. **GNOME:** Official desktop of the GNU Project; comprehensive and user-friendly.
  2. **UKUI:** Lightweight, agile Linux desktop developed by the **Kylin Software** team based on GTK and QT with minimal component dependencies.
  3. **DDE (Deepin Desktop Environment):** Powerful desktop environment developed by the **UnionTech Software** team.
  4. **Kiran:** Secure, stable, efficient desktop developed by the **Hunan Kylin Information Security** team; supports both **x86 and AArch64**.
  5. **XFCE:** Lightweight Linux desktop updated from GTK2 to GTK3 and GDBus with Object Introspection (GI).

---

### 2. Local Virtual Consoles, Remote Login & Shell Prompts
* **Local Login & Virtual Consoles:**
  * A typical Linux system provides **six virtual consoles (`tty1` to `tty6`)** and one graphical console.
  * Press **`Ctrl+Alt+F[1–6]`** (or **`Alt+F1` to `Alt+F6`** in text mode) to switch between the 6 independent virtual consoles. If a program deadlocks on one console, you can switch to another virtual console to kill it.
* **Remote Login:** Enabled by default via SSH using terminal clients like **PuTTY** or **Xshell**.
* **Shell & System Prompt:**
  * A **Shell** (compiled in C) acts as the bridge between the user and the Linux kernel. Common shells include **`bash`** (default on openEuler), `sh`, `csh`, and `ksh`.
  * Prompt format: `[Current login user@Host name Current location]#/$`
  * **`#` (Hash/Pound):** Indicates the **root** superuser (`[root@openEuler ~]#`).
  * **`` (Dollar sign):** Indicates a **common (regular) user** (`[user@openEuler ~]`).
  * Use **`su - username`** to switch users, and **`id`** to check the current user's UID/GID.

---

### 3. Essential Bash Shell Keyboard Shortcuts
| Shortcut / Command | Function in Bash Shell |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`Tab`** | **Automatically supplements (auto-completes) commands, parameters, or file names** (Ch.02 Quiz Q2!). Press **`Tab` twice** on an empty line to list all available commands. |

lecture.title: Linux Command Syntax, Help Utilities & Session/Power Management
objectives: Parse standard Linux command syntax (`command [-option] [parameter]`) and distinguish short (`-a`) vs. long (`--all`) options
Query documentation using `man` (9 manual sections and `coreutils-help` on openEuler), `whatis`, and `help`
Execute login/session commands (`login`, `last`, `exit`) and safe power management (`shutdown`, `halt`, `reboot`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Why CLI & Standard Linux Command Syntax
* **Why CLI:** Higher efficiency (keyboard + scripting automation), low resource overhead compared to GUI, and often the only choice for production servers.
* **Standard Syntax:** `command [-option] [parameter]` (e.g., `ls -la /etc`).
  * Multiple short options can be combined after a single hyphen (`-la` = `-l -a`).
  * **Short options** use one hyphen (`-a`); **long options** use two hyphens (`--all`).

---

### 2. Help Utilities: `man`, `whatis`, and `help`
* **`man` (Manual Pages — part of the `man-db` package):**
  * Searches for `.gz` manual files in `/usr/share/man`.
  * **openEuler Streamlining Rule:** On openEuler, command binaries and documentation packages are separated! Installing a command does not automatically install its man pages; you must install **`coreutils-help`** to view detailed manuals for core commands.
  * **9 Manual Sections:**
    * **`1`**: User commands/programs operable in the shell (e.g., `man 1 passwd`).
    * **`2`**: System calls invoked by the kernel.
    * **`3`**: Library functions (e.g., `man 3 sleep`).
    * **`4`**: Device file descriptions (usually in `/dev`).
    * **`5`**: File formats and conventions (e.g., `man 5 passwd` for `/etc/passwd`).
    * **`6`**: Games.
    * **`7`**: Miscellaneous (macros, conventions).
    * **`8`**: System management commands (root/superuser only).
    * **`9`**: Kernel routines (non-standard).
  * Search man pages by keyword: **`man -k KEYWORD`** or `find /usr/share/man -iname "*KEYWORD*"`.
* **`whatis <command>`:** Pulls the `NAME` section from a manual page to display a one-line summary (e.g., `whatis ls` -> `ls (1) - list directory contents`).
* **`help [-d|-s] <builtin>`:** Displays help for Bash built-in commands (e.g., `help pwd`). `-d` prints a brief description; `-s` prints command syntax.

---

### 3. Login/Session & Power Management Commands
* **Login & Session Auditing:**
  * **`login`**: Logs in to the system (applicable to all users).
  * **`last`**: Reads `/var/log/wtmp` to display recent user/terminal logins, reboots, and shutdowns. Options: `-n <num>` (number of records), `-t tty` (specific console), `-y` (display year/month/day), `-x` (shutdowns/logins/logouts), `-f file`, `-i IP`.
  * **`exit`**: Logs out of the current shell session (no options).
* **Power Management (Superuser Only):**
  * **`shutdown`**: Safely shuts down or restarts the system, notifying all logged-in users and freezing `login`.
    * **`-h`**: Powers off after shutdown.
    * **`-r`**: Restarts after shutdown.
    * **`-k`**: Sends warning messages to users **without** actually shutting down.
    * **`-F`**: Forcibly runs filesystem check (`fsck`) on reboot.
    * **`-t <sec>` / `-time`**: Specifies delay before shutdown.
  * **`halt`**: Terminates processes, calls `sync` (writes buffer data to disk), and stops the kernel. Options: `-n` (do not sync system calls—used after repairing root partition with `fsck` so kernel doesn't overwrite repaired superblock), `-w` (only write record to `/var/log/wtmp` without halting), `-d` (do not write record to `wtmp`), `-f` (force halt without calling `shutdown`), `-i` (shut down network interfaces first).
  * **`reboot`**: Restarts the host (`-n`, `-w`, `-d`, `-i`).
key_takeaways: man pages are divided into 9 sections: 1 = User commands, 2 = System calls, 3 = C library functions, 4 = /dev devices, 5 = Config file formats, 8 = Root admin commands.
On openEuler, command packages and documentation packages are separated; install 'coreutils-help' to access core command manual pages.
shutdown -k only broadcasts a warning without shutting down; halt -w / reboot -w only writes a record to /var/log/wtmp without halting/rebooting.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: 'man 1 passwd' views the passwd command manual, whereas 'man 5 passwd' views the /etc/passwd configuration file format manual!
EXAM TRAP: Neither 'shutdown -k', 'halt -w', nor 'reboot -w' actually powers off or restarts the server—'-k' only warns users, and '-w' only writes a test record to /var/log/wtmp.

lecture.title: Linux File Directory Structure (FHS) & Path Navigation (`pwd`, `cd`, `ls`)
objectives: Apply the Linux philosophy 'Everything is a file' and identify the purpose of every standard root subdirectory (`/bin`, `/sbin`, `/etc`, `/proc`, `/var`, `/dev`, `/usr`, `/opt`, etc.)
Differentiate absolute paths vs. relative paths and logical (`pwd -L`) vs. physical (`pwd -P`) working directories
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. "Everything is a File" & Linux Directory Tree (`/`)
In Linux, **everything is a file**—regular files, directories, character/block devices, sockets, pipes, and processes can all be read/written via `fopen()`, `fclose()`, `fwrite()`, and `fread()`. All directories branch from the single **root directory (`/`)**:

| Directory | Purpose & Key Characteristics |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`/bin` & `/sbin`** | `/bin` stores frequently used binary commands for all users; `/sbin` (`s` = superuser) stores system management programs for `root`. |
| **`/boot`** | Core files for starting the Linux OS (kernel images, bootloader, initramfs). |
| **`/dev`** | External hardware device files (disks, terminals) accessed just like files. |
| **`/etc`** | All system and service configuration files and subdirectories. |
| **`/home` & `/root`** | `/home` contains regular users' home directories (`/home/username`); `/root` is the superuser's home directory. |
| **`/lib` & `/lib64`** | Essential dynamic link libraries (similar to Windows `.dll` files) and 64-bit shared libraries. |
| **`/media` & `/mnt`** | `/media` auto-mounts removable media (USB drives, CD-ROMs); `/mnt` is for temporary manual mounts. |
| **`/opt`** | Optional/additional third-party application software (empty by default). |
| **`/proc`** | **Virtual directory that is a mapping of system memory (RAM).** Access it directly to obtain real-time kernel/process information. |
| **`/run`** | Temporary file system storing runtime data since boot (cleared on reboot; `/var/run` points to `/run`). |
| **`/srv` & `/sys`** | `/srv` stores service data; `/sys` mounts `sysfs` (introduced in Linux 2.6 kernel for hardware/kernel objects). |
| **`/tmp` & `/var`** | `/tmp` stores temporary files; `/var` stores constantly expanding variable files such as **logs (`/var/log`)**. |
| **`/usr`** | User applications and files (similar to Windows `Program Files`). |

---

### 2. Paths, `pwd`, and `cd`
* **Absolute Path:** Always starts from the root slash **`/`** (e.g., `/var/log/messages`).
* **Relative Path:** Relative to the current working directory (e.g., `../lib` or `./script.sh`).
* **`pwd` (Print Working Directory):**
  * **`pwd -L` (Default):** Prints the **logical** path (preserves symbolic link names from `$PWD`).
  * **`pwd -P`:** Prints the **physical** directory path, resolving all symbolic links!
* **`cd` (Change Directory):**
  * `cd` or `cd ~`: Goes to the current user's home directory.
  * `cd ..`: Moves to the upper-level (parent) directory.
  * `cd .`: Stays in the current directory.
  * **`cd -`**: Switches back to the **previous working directory** (fast toggle between two directories).

---

### 3. Listing Files and Directories with `ls`
* **`-l`**: Long format (file type, permissions, hard links, owner, group, size, timestamp, name).
* **`-a` vs. `-A`**: **`-a`** shows all hidden files (starting with `.`) **including `.` and `..`**; **`-A`** shows hidden files **excluding `.` and `..`**.
* **`-h`**: Human-readable sizes (`4.0K`, `12M`, `2G`).
* **`-d`**: Displays information about the **directory itself** (`ls -ld /etc`) rather than its contents.
* **Sorting flags:** **`-t`** (sort by modification/creation time), **`-S`** (sort by size), **`-X`** (sort by extension), **`-r`** (reverse sort order), **`-R`** (recursive listing).
key_takeaways: /proc is a virtual directory that maps system memory (RAM); /var stores constantly growing files like logs; /etc stores configuration files.
pwd -L (default) prints the logical symlink path, whereas pwd -P resolves symlinks and prints the true physical directory path.
ls -a includes '.' and '..', whereas ls -A excludes them; ls -ld <dir> inspects the directory itself rather than listing its contents.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse /root (the home directory of the superuser) with / (the root directory of the entire Linux filesystem tree)!
EXAM TRAP: If /tmp/link3 points to /tmp/d1 and you run 'cd /tmp/link3', 'pwd' (or 'pwd -L') outputs '/tmp/link3', whereas 'pwd -P' outputs '/tmp/d1'.

lecture.title: File & Directory Creation, Copying, Moving & Deletion (`mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`)
objectives: Create single, multiple, and nested parent directories with `mkdir [-p] [-v]` and manage file timestamps with `touch [-a|-m|-t|-d]`
Copy files and directories while preserving attributes or creating links with `cp [-a|-p|-r|-l|-s|-i]`
Move/rename files with `mv [-b|-f|-i|-u]` and safely remove files/directories with `rm [-r|-f|-i|-v]`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Creating Directories (`mkdir`) and Files/Timestamps (`touch`)
* **`mkdir [OPTION]... DIRECTORY...` (Make Directory):**
  * Creates one (`mkdir dir1`) or multiple directories (`mkdir dir1 dir2`).
  * **`-p` (Parents):** Creates non-existent parent directories automatically (`mkdir -p dir1/dir2/dir3`) and **suppresses errors** if the directory already exists.
  * **`-v` (Verbose):** Displays a message for each created directory (`mkdir -pv dir1/dir2`).
* **`touch [OPTION]... FILE...`:**
  * Creates an empty file if it does not exist, or updates its timestamps if it already exists:
    * **`touch file`:** Updates all timestamps to the current system time.
    * **`touch -a file`:** Changes **only the access time (atime)**.
    * **`touch -m file`:** Changes **only the modification time (mtime)**.
    * **`touch -d "2020-01-17 17:14:10" file`:** Sets the timestamp using a date string.
    * **`touch -t 202001020304.05 file`:** Sets the timestamp using `[[CC]YY]MMDDhhmm[.ss]` format.

---

### 2. Copying Files and Directories (`cp`)
* **Syntax:** `cp [OPTION]... SOURCE... DIRECTORY` or `cp [OPTION]... [-T] SOURCE DEST`
* **Key Options:**
  * **`-r`:** Recursively copies directories and all subdirectories/files.
  * **`-p`:** Preserves file content, modification time, ownership, and access permissions.
  * **`-a` (Archive):** Retains links, file attributes, and copies block/character devices and pipe files intact (`-dpR`).
  * **`-l` vs. `-s`:** **`-l`** creates a **hard link** instead of copying data; **`-s`** creates a **symbolic (soft) link** (`cp -s /etc/passwd passwd_link`).
  * **`-t DIRECTORY SOURCE...`:** Specifies target directory first (ideal with `xargs`: `find -name "*.html" | xargs cp -t /data/html/`).
  * **Root Alias Note:** In openEuler's default root shell, `cp`, `mv`, and `rm` are aliased with **`-i` (interactive prompt)** to prevent accidental overwriting. Note that in `cp`, `-f` deletes an unopenable destination file and retries, rather than bypassing the `cp -i` alias prompt.

---

### 3. Moving/Renaming (`mv`) and Deleting (`rm`)
* **`mv [option] source target` (Move / Rename):**
  * Moves files/directories across directories, or **renames** a file if source and target are in the same parent directory (`mv test02.log test03.log`).
  * **`-f`:** Forcibly overwrites target without prompting.
  * **`-i`:** Prompts for user consent before overwriting. (**Rule:** If both `-i` and `-f` are specified on `mv` or `rm`, **the option on the right (last option) takes effect**!)
  * **`-b`:** Backs up the target file before overwriting.
  * **`-u`:** Updates the target file **only when the source file is newer** than the target.
* **`rm [OPTION] file_or_dir` (Remove):**
  * **Irreversible Deletion:** Linux `rm` does **not** move files to a recycle bin; deleted files cannot be restored easily.
  * **`-r` / `-R` / `--recursive`:** Recursively deletes directories and all contents.
  * **`-f` / `--force`:** Ignores non-existent files and deletes without prompting (`rm -rf dir1`).
  * **`-i`:** Interactive confirmation before each deletion.
key_takeaways: mkdir -p automatically creates missing parent directories and reports no error if the target directory already exists.
cp -a preserves all attributes, symlinks, and special device files; cp -p preserves mode, ownership, and timestamps; cp -s creates a symbolic link.
In mv and rm, the shell aliases include -i by default; if both -i and -f are passed on the command line, the rightmost option takes effect.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: To copy or delete a directory, you MUST include '-r' (or '-a' for cp). Running 'cp dir1 dir2' or 'rm dir1' without '-r' fails!
EXAM TRAP: 'touch -a' updates only the access time, whereas 'touch -m' updates only the modification time.

lecture.title: File Search (`find`, `locate`, `which`), Compression (`gzip`, `tar`) & Links (`ln`)
objectives: Search files in real time with `find` (`-name`, `-type`, `-mtime`, `-user`, `-size`, `-empty`, `-exec`), index-based `locate`/`updatedb`, and `$PATH`-based `which`
Compress and archive files using `gzip` (60–70% compression ratio) and `tar` (`-c`, `-x`, `-t`, `-z`, `-j`, `-J`, `-v`, `-f`, `-C`)
Compare and create hard links (`ln`) vs. symbolic/soft links (`ln -s`) and trace their behavior when source files are deleted
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. File Search Utilities: `find`, `locate`, and `which`
* **`find [path...] [expression]` (Real-time directory traversal):**
  * **`-name "pattern"` / `-iname`:** Search by filename (case-sensitive / case-insensitive).
  * **`-type <c>`:** Filter by file type: **`f`** (general file), **`d`** (directory), **`l`** (symbolic link), **`b`** (block device), **`c`** (character device), **`p`** (named pipe).
  * **`-mtime -n / +n`:** By modification time (`-7` = within last 7 days; **`+7` = earlier than 7 days ago**).
  * **`-user <uname>` / `-perm <mode>` / `-size <N>`:** By owner, permission, or size.
  * **`-empty [-delete]`:** Finds (and optionally deletes) empty files/directories.
  * **`-exec cmd {} \;`:** Runs `cmd` on each matched file (e.g., `find -name "*.html" -exec cp {} /data/html/ \;`).
* **`locate [OPTION] PATTERN` (Fast database index search):**
  * Searches the pre-built index database `/var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db`.
  * **Must run `updatedb` first** if the database does not exist or newly created files are not yet indexed!
* **`which [-a] programname`:** Searches only directories in **`PATH`** to find the absolute path of an executable command (`-a` lists all matches across `PATH`).

---

### 2. Compression & Archiving: `gzip` and `tar`
* **`gzip [option] [file/dir]`:**
  * Compresses files in place with a **60% to 70% compression ratio** for text files, appending **`.gz`** and replacing the original file.
  * Options: **`-d`** (decompress, equivalent to `gunzip`), **`-l`** (list compressed/uncompressed sizes & ratio), **`-r`** (recursively compress files in subdirectories), **`-v`** (verbose), **`-f`** (force).
* **`tar [OPTION...] [FILE]` (Tape Archive — packs multiple files/directories):**
  * **Action flags:** **`-c`** (create archive), **`-x`** (extract archive), **`-t`** (list contents without extracting).
  * **Compression filter flags:**
    * **`-z`:** `gzip` (`.tar.gz` / `.tgz`)
    * **`-j`:** `bzip2` (`.tar.bz2`)
    * **`-J`:** `xz` (`.tar.xz`)
  * **Helper flags:** **`-v`** (verbose), **`-f <archive_name>`** (must immediately precede archive filename), **`-C <target_dir>`** (extract to specified directory instead of current directory).

---

### 3. Hard Links vs. Soft (Symbolic) Links (`ln`)
By default, **`ln Source Target` creates a hard link**; adding **`-s`** (`ln -s Source Target`) creates a **soft (symbolic) link**:

| Feature | Soft Link (`ln -s`) | Hard Link (`ln` default) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nature** | A path shortcut (like a Windows shortcut); has its own new inode (`lrwxrwxrwx`). | A file entry pointing to the **exact same inode/data blocks**; does not occupy extra disk space. |
| **If Source File is Deleted** | **Becomes invalid (broken/dangling link)!** | **No impact!** Data remains accessible via the hard link (`link count` decreases by 1). |
| **Linking to Directories** | **Supported** | **Not supported** (by default; prevents directory loops). |
| **Cross-File System Linking** | **Supported** | **Not supported** (inodes are unique per filesystem). |
key_takeaways: find /var/log/anaconda/ -type f -mtime +7 searches for regular files modified more than 7 days ago; locate requires updatedb to update /var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db.
tar -zcf packs with gzip (.tar.gz), tar -jcf uses bzip2 (.tar.bz2), tar -Jcf uses xz (.tar.xz), and -C specifies the extraction target directory.

ln creates a hard link by default (survives source file deletion, cannot cross filesystems or link directories); ln -s creates a soft/symbolic link (breaks if source is deleted, can link directories and cross filesystems).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: If you create a soft link 'ln -s passwd link_s', delete 'passwd', and then copy a new 'passwd' back to the same name, the soft link 'link_s' works again (points by path), whereas a hard link 'link_h' still points to the old inode and is no longer synchronized with the new 'passwd' file (Ch.03 p.117)!
EXAM TRAP: gzip has a 60%–70% compression ratio for text files and replaces the original file with file.gz.

quiz_questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately compare soft links (`ln -s`) and hard links (`ln`) on Linux?

lecture.title: Vim Text Editor Modes, Navigation, Editing & Search/Replace
objectives: Distinguish Vi vs. Vim (Bram Moolenaar, 1991) and navigate its basic modes (Normal, Insert, Visual, Select, Command-line, Ex) and derivative modes
Execute Vim CLI launch options (`-c`, `-R`, `-M`, `-r`, `+num`, `-`, `-t`, `-q`) and Normal-mode cursor/data commands (`gg`, `G`, `yy`, `dd`, `p`, `u`, `U`, `Ctrl+R`)
Perform Command-line mode operations: line numbering (`:set nu`/`nonu`), search highlighting (`:set hlsearch`), regex substitution (`:%s/old/new/gi`), and saving/exiting (`:wq`, `:q!`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Vi vs. Vim and Editor Modes
* **Vi & Vim Evolution:** **Vi** is the universal standard Unix text editor with three basic modes (Command, Insert, Visual). **Vim** was released in **1991 by Bram Moolenaar** (initially *Vi IMitation*, later renamed **Vi IMproved**). Note: After a minimal openEuler installation, you may need to manually install `vim`.
* **Vim Modes:**
  * **6 Basic Modes:** **Normal** (default startup mode for cursor movement and operator commands), **Insert** (entered via `i` or `a`; press `ESC` to return to Normal mode), **Visual** (highlights characters/lines/blocks for operators), **Select** (Windows-like selection where typing replaces highlighted text and enters Insert mode), **Command-line** (`:`, `/`, `?`, `!`), and **Ex** (batch command mode; exit with `:visual`).
  * **5 Derivative Modes:** **Operator-pending** (waiting for text object like `aw` word, `as` sentence, `ap` paragraph), **Insert Normal** (`Ctrl+O` in Insert mode executes one Normal command then returns to Insert), **Insert Visual**, **Insert Select**, and **Replace** (press **`R`** in Normal mode to overwrite characters).
  * **Other:** **eVim** (`evim` or `vim -y` — modeless GUI mode staying in Insert mode).

---

### 2. Vim CLI Launch Options & Normal Mode Keybindings
* **CLI Syntax & Options (`vim [options] [file]...`):**
  * **`+num`**: Opens file with cursor at line `num`.
  * **`-R` vs. `-M`**: **`-R`** opens in read-only mode (can still force save with `:w!`); **`-M`** opens in strict read-only mode (**does not allow forcible saving**).
  * **`-r`**: Recovers a crashed session (swap file).
  * **`-c <cmd>`**: Runs specified command before opening file; **`-`** reads from `stdin`; **`-t tag`** jumps to tag definition; **`-q [errorfile]`** jumps to first error.

| Category | Normal / Command-Line Mode Keybindings |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Cursor Movement** | `k` (up), `j` (down), `h` (left), `l` (right); **`0`** (beginning of line); **`g0`** (leftmost character on screen); **`gg`** (first line of file); **`G`** (last line of file); **`:n`** (jump to line `n`). |
| **Copy, Cut & Paste** | **`yy` or `Y`** (copy entire line); **`y[n]w`** (copy `n` words); **`[n]dd`** (delete/cut `n` lines; `2dd` equals `dj`); **`d[n]w`** (delete `n` words); **`p`** (paste below line / after cursor); **`P`** (paste above line / before cursor). |
| **Undo & Redo** | **`u`** (undo latest change); **`U`** (undo **all changes on the current line** since cursor arrived on it); **`Ctrl+R`** (redo last undo). |

---

### 3. Line Numbers, Search/Replace & Saving/Exiting
* **Line Numbers & Search Highlighting:**
  * **`:set nu`** (display line numbers) / **`:set nonu`** (hide line numbers).
  * **`:set hlsearch`** (temporarily highlight search matches; add `set hlsearch` to **`/etc/vimrc`** for permanent configuration).
* **Find & Replace:**
  * **`/word`** (search forwards) and **`?word`** (search backwards). Press **`n`** for next match, **`N`** for previous match.
  * **`:1,5s/word1/word2/g`**: Replaces all `word1` with `word2` in lines 1 to 5 (without `g`, only the first match per line is replaced).
  * **`:%s/word1/word2/gi`**: Replaces all occurrences across the entire file (`%`), case-insensitively (`i`).
* **Saving & Exiting:** **`:w`** (save), **`:q`** (quit), **`:wq`** (save and quit), **`:q!`** (force quit without saving), **`:wq!`** (force save and quit).
key_takeaways: Vim starts in Normal mode by default; press 'i' or 'a' to enter Insert mode, 'R' for Replace mode, 'Ctrl+O' in Insert mode for one-shot Insert Normal mode, and 'ESC' to return to Normal mode.
In Normal mode: 'gg' = first line, 'G' = last line, 'yy' = copy line, '[n]dd' = delete n lines, 'u' = undo last change, 'U' = undo all changes on current line, 'Ctrl+R' = redo.
In Command-line mode: ':set nu' shows line numbers, ':set hlsearch' highlights matches (persisted in /etc/vimrc), and ':%s/old/new/gi' replaces globally and case-insensitively.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Distinguishing 'vim -R' vs. 'vim -M': '-R' opens a file in read-only mode but allows forcible saving (:wq!), whereas '-M' opens in read-only mode and DOES NOT allow forcible saving!
EXAM TRAP: In Vim, lowercase 'u' undoes the single latest change, whereas uppercase 'U' undoes ALL changes made on the current line, and 'Ctrl+R' redoes an undone change.

lecture.title: File Viewing & Extraction (`cat`, `more`, `less`, `head`, `tail`)
objectives: View and concatenate files with `cat` (`-n`, `-b`, `-s`, `-E`, `-A`)
Compare paginated viewers `more` (loads entire file upfront) vs. `less` (loads on demand, bidirectional scrolling & search)
Extract file headers and tails using `head` (first 10 lines by default — Ch.03 Quiz!) and `tail` (last 10 lines by default, `-f` real-time log tracking)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Viewing & Combining Files with `cat`
`cat` reads entire files to standard output, creates files (`cat > filename`), or combines files (`cat file1 file2 > file3`):
* **`-n` (`--number`):** Numbers **all** output lines starting from 1.
* **`-b` (`--number-nonblank`):** Numbers **only non-empty (non-blank)** lines starting from 1.
* **`-s`:** Squeezes multiple consecutive blank lines into a single blank line.
* **`-E` (`--show-ends`):** Appends **`$`** at the end of each line.
* **`-A` (`--show-all`):** Equivalent to **`-vET`**; displays all non-printable characters (tabs, line endings).

---

### 2. Paginated Viewing: `more` vs. `less`
| Feature / Key | `more [options] <file>` | `less [option] file` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Loading Mechanism** | Reads from front to back and **loads the entire file from the very start**. | **Does NOT load the entire file** before displaying; faster on huge logs and more flexible (Vim-like UI). |
| **CLI Options** | **`+n`** (start at line `n`), **`-n`** (set screen size to `n` lines), **`-c`** (clear screen from top), **`-s`** (squeeze blank lines), **`+/pattern`** (search pattern before displaying). | **`-N`** (show line numbers), **`-i`** (ignore case in search), **`-s`** (squeeze blank lines), **`-f`** (force open special/binary file), **`-o <file>`** (save output to file), **`-g`** (highlight only last match). |
| **Interactive Keys** | `Space` / `Ctrl+F` (next page), `Enter` (next line), `b` / `Ctrl+B` (previous page), **`=`** (print current line number), **`:f`** (print filename & line number), **`v`** (invoke `vi`), **`!cmd`** (run shell cmd), **`q`** (quit). | `/string` (search down), `?string` (search up), `n`/`N` (repeat search), `b`/`PageUp` (prev page), `d` (down half page), `u` (up half page), `y` (prev line), `h` (help), `q`/`Q` (quit). |

---

### 3. Extracting File Beginnings (`head`) and Ends (`tail`)
* **`head [option]... [file]...`:**
  * **Default Behavior (Official Ch.03 Quiz Q1!):** Displays the **first 10 lines** of a file by default!
  * **`-n num` / `-c num`:** Displays the first `num` lines / bytes (`head -n 3 /etc/passwd`).
  * **Negative Count (`head -n -num` / `head -c -num`):** Displays **all lines/bytes EXCEPT the last `num` lines/bytes** (e.g., `head -n -40 /etc/passwd` outputs everything except the last 40 lines!).
  * **`-q` / `-v`:** Hide (`-q`, default for single file) or display (`-v`) the filename header.
* **`tail [option]... [file]...`:**
  * **Default Behavior:** Displays the **last 10 lines** of a file by default.
  * **`-n num` / `-c num`:** Displays the last `num` lines / bytes (`tail -n 3 /etc/passwd`).
  * **Plus Offset (`tail -n +num` / `tail -c +num`):** Reads data **starting from the `num`-th line/byte to the end of the file** (`tail -n +3 file`).
  * **`-f`:** **Reads log files cyclically in real time** (traces growing log files like `tail -f ping.log`).
key_takeaways: By default, both 'head' and 'tail' display 10 lines (the first 10 lines and last 10 lines, respectively — Ch.03 Quiz Q1).

lecture.title: Text Extraction, Filtering, Statistics & Sorting (`cut`, `grep`, `wc`, `sort`, `diff`, `tr`)
objectives: Slice columns and character ranges using `cut` (`-b`, `-c`, `-d`, `-f` with ranges `N-`, `N-M`, `-M`)
Filter lines with `grep` (`-c`, `-i`, `-w`, `-x`) and compute line/word/byte counts with `wc` (`-l`, `-w`, `-c`)
Sort, deduplicate, compare, and translate text streams using `sort` (`-n`, `-r`, `-u`, `-o`), `diff` (`-B`, `-c`, `-i`, `-r`, `-w`), and `tr` (`-c`, `-d`, `-s`, `-t`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Column Extraction (`cut`) & Keyword Filtering (`grep`)
* **`cut [option]... [file]` (Extract columns/fields):**
  * **`-d <char>`:** Specifies the field separator (**default separator is `TAB`**). Example: `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd`.
  * **`-f [range]`:** Selects fields (multiple fields separated by commas `,`).
  * **`-b [range]` / `-c [range]`:** Selects bytes (`-b`) or characters (`-c`).
  * **Range Syntax:** **`N-`** (from `N`-th to end), **`N-M`** (from `N`-th to `M`-th inclusive), **`-M`** (from 1st to `M`-th inclusive).
* **`grep [option] pattern [file]...` (Regular expression line search):**
  * Enclose multi-word patterns in single or double quotes so words after the first aren't misinterpreted as filenames!
  * **`-c`:** Prints only the **count** of matching lines.
  * **`-i`:** Ignores case sensitivity.
  * **`-w`:** Matches **whole words** only.
  * **`-x`:** Matches only results spanning the **whole line**.

---

### 2. Text Statistics (`wc`) & Sorting (`sort`)
* **`wc [option]... [file]...` (Word/Line/Byte Count):**
  * Reads from `stdin` if no file or `-` is given.
  * **`-l` (`--lines`):** Displays only the number of **lines**.
  * **`-w` (`--words`):** Displays only the number of **words**.
  * **`-c` (`--bytes` / `--chars`):** Displays only the number of **bytes**.
* **`sort [option]... [file]...` (Line Sorting):**
  * **`-n`:** Sorts **numerically** by value (instead of ASCII character order).
  * **`-r`:** Sorts in **reverse** (descending) order.
  * **`-u`:** Ignores repeated lines (**unique**).
  * **`-o <file>`:** Saves sorted output directly to `<file>`.
  * **`-b`** (ignore leading spaces), **`-c`** (check if already sorted), **`-d`** (letters, digits, spaces only), **`-f`** (fold lowercase into uppercase).

---

### 3. File Comparison (`diff`) & Character Translation (`tr`)
* **`diff [option]... file1 file2` (Line-by-line Comparison):**
  * If directories are specified, `diff` compares files with the same name in those directories (non-recursively unless `-r` is passed).
  * **`-B`** (ignore blank lines), **`-c`** (context format marking differences), **`-i`** (ignore case), **`-r`** (compare subdirectories recursively), **`-w`** (ignore all whitespace).
* **`tr [option]... set1 [set2]` (Character Translation/Deletion from `stdin`):**
  * Reads **only from standard input (`stdin`)**, converts or deletes characters, and writes to `stdout` (e.g., `cat text.txt | tr a-z A-Z`).
  * **`-d`:** **Deletes** characters in `set1`.
  * **`-s`:** **Squeezes** consecutive repeated characters into a single character.
  * **`-c`:** Inverts (complements) `set1` (processes characters *not* in `set1`).
  * **`-t`:** Truncates `set1` to the length of `set2`.
key_takeaways: In 'cut', the default delimiter is TAB; use '-d:' and '-f1' to extract the first colon-separated column of /etc/passwd.
grep -c counts matching lines, -i ignores case, -w matches whole words, and -x matches whole lines; wc -l, -w, -c count lines, words, and bytes.
sort -n sorts numerically, -r reverses order, -u removes duplicate lines; tr reads from stdin (e.g., cat file | tr a-z A-Z) and uses -d to delete characters.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: The default field separator of 'cut' is TAB, whereas the default field separator of 'awk' is spaces/whitespace!
EXAM TRAP: 'tr' does NOT accept a filename as a command-line argument—it reads from standard input (stdin) via a pipe ('|') or input redirection ('<').

lecture.title: Advanced Stream Processing with `awk` and `sed`
objectives: Analyze and slice text streams line-by-line using `awk` (`0`, `1..$n`, default space separator, `-F` custom field delimiter)
Understand how `sed` (stream editor) processes lines in a pattern buffer without altering the original file by default
Apply `sed` options (`-n`, `-e`, `-f`, `-i`, `-l`, `-r`) for non-interactive string replacement and in-place file editing
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Column & Pattern Analysis with `awk`
**`awk`** is a powerful text analysis utility that reads files or standard input **line by line**, slices each line into fields using **spaces (whitespace) as the default separator**, and executes actions on each slice.
* **Syntax:** `awk [options] 'action' filename`
* **Positional Field Variables:**
  * **`0`**: Represents the **entire current line** (e.g., `awk '{print 0}' test.txt`).
  * **`1`, `2`, `$3`...**: Represent the 1st, 2nd, 3rd field of the current line.
* **Custom Field Separator (`-F`):**
  * Use `-F` to specify a delimiter other than whitespace, such as `:` for `/etc/passwd`:
    ```bash
    awk -F: '{print 1, 3}' /etc/passwd
    ```
* **Pipeline Example from Official Material (Ch.03, p.144):**
  ```bash
  # Display the last five accounts that have logged in to the system:
  [root@openEuler ~]# last -n 5 | awk '{print $1}'
  ```

---

### 2. Non-Interactive Stream Editing with `sed`
**`sed`** is a streamlined, **non-interactive** stream editor capable of modifying character strings across standard input or files (unlike `tr`, which only performs character-level mapping).
* **Buffer Execution Principle:**
  * When `sed` runs, it reads one line at a time from the input into a **temporary memory buffer (pattern space)**, applies the editing commands to the buffer copy, prints the buffer to `stdout`, and moves to the next line.
  * **Crucial Rule:** By default, **`sed` only modifies the copied text in the buffer and leaves the original file untouched!** To modify the original file directly on disk, you **must pass `-i`**.

---

### 3. Key `sed` Options & Actions
| Option / Action | Description & Usage |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`-n`** | **Cancels default output** (only prints lines explicitly marked with the `p` action, e.g., `sed -n '1,5p' file`). |
| **`-e <script>`** | Specifies **multipoint editing**, allowing multiple `sed` subcommands in a single invocation. |
| **`-f <file>`** | Reads `sed` editing commands from a script file. |
| **`-i`** | **Directly edits the original file in place** (instead of only outputting modified buffer text to `stdout`). |
| **`-l <N>`** | Specifies the line-wrap length for the `l` command. |
| **`-r`** | Uses **extended regular expressions (ERE)** in the script. |
| **`s/old/new/g`** | Substitutes `old` with `new` globally on matched lines; **`d`** deletes matched lines; **`a`/`i`/`c`** appends/inserts/changes lines. |
key_takeaways: awk reads input line by line using spaces as the default separator; 0 is the entire line, 1 is the first field, and -F changes the field separator.
sed is a non-interactive stream editor that modifies text in a memory buffer by default without changing the source file on disk.
In sed, -i edits the original file directly in place, -n suppresses default output, -e enables multipoint editing, and -r enables extended regular expressions.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Running 'sed "s/foo/bar/g" file.txt' does NOT modify file.txt on disk—it only prints the modified buffer to standard output! You must use 'sed -i' to edit the original file directly.
EXAM TRAP: Remember the difference between 'tr' and 'sed': 'tr' performs single-character translation/deletion from stdin, whereas 'sed' modifies character strings and lines.

lecture.title: User & Group Architecture (UID/GID) and Configuration Files
objectives: Distinguish the three Linux user types by UID range: Superuser (0), Virtual/System user (1–999), and Common/Regular user (1000–60000)
Compare Private (primary/owner) groups vs. Public (additional/supplementary) groups
Parse every colon-delimited field of `/etc/passwd` (7 fields) and `/etc/group` (4 fields) along with `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/gshadow`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Linux User Types (UID) and Group Types (GID)
When a user logs in to Linux, the system identifies the user type by **UID (User ID)**, not by the username!
* **Three User Categories by UID Range (Ch.04, p.160):**
  1. **Superuser (`root`):** **`UID = 0`** (and `GID = 0`). Has full control over the entire OS.
  2. **Virtual user (System user):** **`UID = 1 to 999`**. Used by background services/daemons; cannot log in interactively with a password (typically uses `/sbin/nologin` or `/usr/sbin/nologin`).
  3. **Common user (Normal/Regular user):** **`UID = 1000 to 60000`**. Can modify files in their own home directory (`/home/username`) and access authorized resources.
* **User Group Relationships:**
  * **Private Group (Owner/Primary Group):** Each user has **only one** private group (created with the same name and GID as the user by default). Newly created files belong to this primary group.
  * **Public Group (Additional/Supplementary Group):** A user can belong to **multiple** public groups to inherit shared permissions.

---

### 2. Structure of `/etc/passwd` (7 Fields) and `/etc/group` (4 Fields)
* **`/etc/passwd` (User Configuration File — 7 Colon-Separated Columns):**
  Example: `root:x:0:0:Super User:/root:/bin/bash`
  1. **Username** (`root`)
  2. **Password placeholder** (`x` — indicates password authentication is required; actual encrypted hashes are stored in `/etc/shadow`)
  3. **UID** (`0`)
  4. **Primary GID** (`0`)
  5. **User description / comment** (`Super User`)
  6. **Home directory** (`/root` or `/home/username`)
  7. **Login shell** (`/bin/bash` for interactive login, or `/sbin/nologin` to forbid shell login)
* **`/etc/group` (Group Configuration File — 4 Colon-Separated Columns):**
  Example: `wheel:x:10:openeuler`
  1. **Group name** (`wheel`)
  2. **Password placeholder** (`x`)
  3. **GID** (`10`)
  4. **Supplementary users list** (Comma-separated list of users for whom this group is a **supplementary/additional group**. Note: If a group is a user's **private/primary group**, the username does **not** appear in the 4th column!).

---

### 3. Companion Account Files
* **`/etc/shadow`:** Stores encrypted user passwords and password aging policies (readable only by `root`).
* **`/etc/gshadow`:** Stores encrypted group passwords and group administrators.
* **`/var/spool/mail/username`:** Stores the user's system mailbox.
key_takeaways: Linux identifies users by UID: 0 = Superuser (root), 1–999 = Virtual (system) users, and 1000–60000 = Common (regular) users.
/etc/passwd has 7 colon-separated fields: username : password_placeholder(x) : UID : GID : description : home_dir : login_shell.
/etc/group has 4 colon-separated fields: group_name : password_placeholder(x) : GID : supplementary_users (private group owners do not appear in column 4).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: The second column 'x' in /etc/passwd is ONLY a password placeholder—the actual encrypted password hash is stored in /etc/shadow!
EXAM TRAP: Each user can have only ONE private (primary) group, but can belong to MULTIPLE public (additional/supplementary) groups.

lecture.title: User, Group & Password Lifecycle Commands (`useradd`, `usermod`, `userdel`, `passwd`, `chage`, `gpasswd`)
objectives: Create, modify, and delete users and groups with `useradd`, `usermod`, `userdel`, `groupadd`, `groupmod`, and `groupdel`
Manage user passwords and account locks with `passwd` (`-n`, `-x`, `-w`, `-i`, `-d`, `-S`, `-l`, `-u`, `-e`) and password aging with `chage` (`-l`, `-M`, `-m`, `-w`, `-d`, `-I`)
Manage group memberships safely without overwriting existing supplementary groups using `gpasswd` (`-a`, `-d`, `-M`, `-A`) vs. `usermod -G`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Creating, Modifying & Deleting Users and Groups
| Command | Key Options & Exam Rules |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`useradd [options] user`** | **`-u`** (specify UID), **`-o`** (used with `-u` to allow duplicate UIDs), **`-g`** (specify basic/primary group name or GID), **`-d`** (specify and create home directory), **`-s`** (specify default login shell), **`-D`** (display/change default config). |
| **`usermod [options] user`** | **`-u`** (modify UID), **`-g`** (modify primary group), **`-G`** (specify supplementary group—**overwrites previous supplementary groups** unless `-a` is combined or `gpasswd -a` is used!), **`-l`** (modify login username), **`-d`** (modify home directory), **`-s`** (modify default shell). |
| **`userdel [options] user`** | Without options, deletes only the account entry (leaves home/mail files). **`-r`** recursively deletes the user **and their home directory/mail files**. **`-f`** forcibly deletes a user even if currently logged in. |
| **`groupadd [options] grp`** | **`-g`** (assign GID), **`-o`** (allow duplicate GID), **`-r`** (create system group), **`-f`** (exit successfully if group exists), **`-p`** (encrypted password). |
| **`groupmod [options] grp`** | **`-g`** (set new GID), **`-n`** (set new group name), **`-o`** (allow duplicate GID), **`-p`** (modify password). |
| **`groupdel [options] grp`** | Deletes a group. **Rule:** If a group is the primary group of an existing user, delete the user first (or use **`-f`** to force). |

---

### 2. Password Management (`passwd`) & Password Aging (`chage`)
* **`passwd [OPTION...] user_name`:** (Root can change any user's password; common users can change only their own.)
  * **`-l` / `-u`:** **Locks (`-l`)** or **unlocks (`-u`)** a user's password.
  * **`-d`:** Deletes a user's password. **`-e`:** Forces immediate password expiration on next login. **`-S`:** Displays password status.
  * **`-n <min>` / `-x <max>` / `-w <warn>` / `-i <inactive>`:** Sets min days, max days, warning days, and grace days before disabling an expired account.
* **`chage [OPTION...] user_name` (Change Age):**
  * **`-l`:** Lists password expiration details for a user.
  * **`-M <days>`:** Maximum password validity period.
  * **`-m <days>`:** Minimum password validity period.
  * **`-w <days>`:** Warning days before password expires.
  * **`-I <days>`:** Inactive days after password expiration before account is locked.
  * **`-d <date/0>`:** Sets last password change date (`-d 0` forces change on next login).

---

### 3. Group Association (`gpasswd`) & `chroot`
* **Why `gpasswd` instead of `usermod -G`?** Running `usermod -G group_name user_name` adds the user to `group_name` **but removes the user from any previous supplementary groups!** To add a user to a group while retaining existing supplementary groups, use **`gpasswd`**.
* **`gpasswd [option] group_name`:**
  * **`-a <user>`:** Adds a user to the group.
  * **`-d <user>`:** Deletes (removes) a user from the group.
  * **`-M <u1,u2>`:** Defines the complete list of group members.
  * **`-A <user>`:** Sets group administrator(s); **`-r`** removes group password; **`-R`** restricts access to members only; **`-Q`** specifies a `chroot` directory.
* **`chroot`:** Changes the apparent root directory (`/`) for a process, enhancing security, isolating development environments, and aiding bootloader/system recovery.
key_takeaways: userdel without options keeps the home directory; 'userdel -r username' deletes both the user account and their home/mail directories.
chage -l lists password aging policy, chage -M sets maximum validity days, and passwd -l / -u locks or unlocks an account.
gpasswd -a user group adds a user to a group while keeping existing supplementary groups, whereas 'usermod -G group user' overwrites previous supplementary groups.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse chage options with passwd options! For maximum password validity days, chage uses uppercase '-M' (chage -M 90 user), whereas passwd uses lowercase '-x' (passwd -x 90 user).
EXAM TRAP: To rename a group, groupmod uses '-n' (groupmod -n newname oldname), whereas to rename a user, usermod uses '-l' (usermod -l newname oldname).

lecture.title: File Types, Permission Bits (`rwx`), Ownership (`chmod`, `chown`, `chgrp`) & `umask`
objectives: Identify all 7 Linux file types (`-`, `d`, `b`, `c`, `l`, `p`, `s`) and decode the 10-character `ls -l` permission string (Bits 0 to 9)
Modify permissions and ownership using `chmod` (symbolic & octal), `chown user:group`, and `chgrp`
Calculate default file and directory permissions from any `umask` value (`022`, `027`, `002`, `006`, `007`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Seven Linux File Types & 10-Bit Permission Structure (`ls -l`)
In `drwxr-xr-x. 2 root root 4096 Jun 1 14:00 shili`, the 10-character mode string is indexed as **Bits 0 to 9**:
* **Bit 0 (File Type — 7 Types in Linux):**
  1. **`-`**: Regular/general file (files excluding the other 6 types).
  2. **`d`**: Directory.
  3. **`b`**: Block device file (random access storage device, e.g., `/dev/sda`).
  4. **`c`**: Character device file (one-time/serial read device such as keyboard and mouse).
  5. **`l`**: Symbolic link file.
  6. **`p`**: Named pipe (FIFO) file.
  7. **`s`**: Socket file.
* **Bits 1–9 (Three 3-Bit Permission Triads):**
  * **Bits 1–3 (`u` — Owner):** File owner permissions.
  * **Bits 4–6 (`g` — Group):** Owner group permissions.
  * **Bits 7–9 (`o` — Others):** Other users' permissions.

| Permission | Octal Value | Meaning on a Regular File (`-`) | Meaning on a Directory (`d`) |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **`r` (Read)** | **4** | Read the actual content of the file. | Read the directory structure list (`ls`). |
| **`w` (Write)** | **2** | Edit, add, or modify file content (does **not** allow deleting the file itself!). | **Create, delete, rename, or move files** inside the directory! |
| **`x` (Execute)** | **1** | Execute the file as a program/script. | **Access/enter the directory (`cd`)**. |

---

### 2. Permission & Ownership Commands: `chmod`, `chown`, `chgrp`
* **`chmod [OPTION]... MODE FILE...` (Usable by file owner or `root`):**
  * **Octal mode:** `chmod 644 usertxt` (`rw-r--r--`), `chmod -R 755 dir`.
  * **Symbolic mode:** Objects `u` (owner), `g` (group), `o` (others), `a` (all) + Operators `+` (add), `-` (remove), `=` (set exact) + Permissions `r`, `w`, `x`.
* **`chown [OPTION]... [OWNER][:[GROUP]] FILE...` (Usable by `root` only):**
  * Changes file owner, owner group, or **both simultaneously**: `chown user:usergroup usertxt`.
  * Options: **`-R`** (recursive), **`-h`** (modify symlink itself), **`-c`** (report only when changed), **`-f`** (ignore errors), **`-v`** (verbose).
* **`chgrp [OPTION]... GROUP FILE...` (Usable by `root`):**
  * Modifies the group to which a file/directory belongs (`chgrp usergroup01 usertxt`, `-R`, `--reference=<file>`).

---

### 3. Preset Permission Mask (`umask`)
`umask [-p] [-S] [mode]` defines the permissions **masked out** when creating a new file (base `666`) or directory (base `777`):

| `umask` Value | Default File Permission | Default Directory Permission |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **`022`** | **`644`** (`rw-r--r--`) | **`755`** (`rwxr-xr-x`) |
| **`027`** | **`640`** (`rw-r-----`) | **`750`** (`rwxr-x---`) |
| **`002`** | **`664`** (`rw-rw-r--`) | **`775`** (`rwxrwxr-x`) |
| **`006`** | **`660`** (`rw-rw----`) | **`771`** (`rwxrwx--x`) |
| **`007`** | **`660`** (`rw-rw----`) | **`770`** (`rwxrwx---`) |
key_takeaways: The 7 Linux file types are '-' (regular), 'd' (directory), 'b' (block device), 'c' (character device), 'l' (symlink), 'p' (named pipe), and 's' (socket).
chmod can be run by the file owner or root, whereas chown can only be run by the administrator (root).
With umask 022, new files get 644 and new directories get 755; with umask 027, new files get 640 and new directories get 750.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Write permission ('w') on a file allows editing its content, NOT deleting the file! Deleting or renaming a file is controlled by write ('w') + execute ('x') permissions on the PARENT DIRECTORY.
EXAM TRAP: Notice 'umask 006' in the official table (Ch.04 p.182): directories get 777 - 006 = 771, while files strip the execute bit to get 660!

lecture.title: Sticky Bit, Access Control Lists (`getfacl`, `setfacl`, `chacl`) & Privilege Escalation (`su`, `sudo`)
objectives: Explain how the Sticky Bit (`drwxrwxrwt`) protects shared directories like `/tmp` and `/share` from unauthorized file deletion
Configure fine-grained Access Control Lists using `getfacl`, `setfacl` (`-m`, `-x`, `-b`, `-k`, `-R`, `-d`), and `chacl` (`-b`, `-d`, `-R`, `-D`, `-B`, `-l`, `-r`)
Compare `su`, `su -`, and `sudo`, and author `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/sudoers.d/username` rules using `visudo`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Sticky Bit (`t`) & Access Control Lists (ACL)
* **Sticky Bit (`drwxrwxrwt`, octal prefix `1`, `chmod o+t`):**
  * Special permission set on shared directories (such as `/tmp` or `/share`).
  * **Rule:** When the Sticky Bit is enabled on a directory, **only the file owner, the directory owner, or the `root` user can rename or remove files within that directory**—even if all users have `rwx` (`777`) permissions on the directory and files!
* **Access Control Lists (ACL):**
  * Solves the limitation of traditional `ugo` (`rwx`) permissions by granting fine-grained permissions to specific individual users or groups.
  * **Indicator:** In `ls -l`, a **plus sign (`+`)** at the end of the permission string (`-rw-rw-r--+`) indicates the file has an ACL configured!
  * **3 ACL Commands:**
    1. **`getfacl [-aceEsRLPtpndvh] file...`:** Obtains ACLs (`-a` file ACL only, `-d` default ACL only, `-c` omit header, `-R` recursive, `-n` numeric UIDs/GIDs).
    2. **`setfacl [-bkndRLP] {-m|-M|-x|-X} file...`:** Sets ACLs:
       * **`-m`:** Modifies/adds an ACL entry (e.g., `setfacl -m u:user1:rwx test`; cannot be combined with `-x`).
       * **`-x`:** Deletes specified ACL entries.
       * **`-b`:** **Deletes ALL extended ACL entries**.
       * **`-k`:** Removes default/preset directory ACL entries; **`-d`** presets default directory ACLs; **`-R`** recursive.
    3. **`chacl`:** Changes file/directory ACLs (`-b` modify file & default dir ACLs, `-d` set default dir ACL, `-R` delete file ACLs only, `-D` delete dir ACLs only, **`-B` delete all ACLs**, `-l` list ACLs, `-r` recursive).

---

### 2. Comparing `su` (`su -`) vs. `sudo`
| Dimension | `su` (substitute user) | `sudo` (superuser do) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basic Function** | Switches user identity (`su` keeps current shell env; **`su -`** switches to target user's login shell env). |Temporarily executes a single command as another user (usually `root`). |
| **Password Required** | **Target user's password** (e.g., `root`'s password). | **Current user's own password** (cached for **5 minutes** by default; unless `NOPASSWD` is set). |
| **Security & Auditing** | Low security: shares root password, broad permissions, **commands are NOT audited/recorded**. | High security: fine-grained command control in `/etc/sudoers`, **every command is logged by default**. |

---

### 3. Configuring `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/sudoers.d/`
* **Best Practice:** Use **`visudo`** (which automatically checks syntax) to edit `/etc/sudoers`, or create a drop-in file **`/etc/sudoers.d/username`** (can be revoked simply by deleting the file).
* **Syntax Breakdown:**
  ```text
  test   openeuler.com=(root)   NOPASSWD:/usr/bin/touch
  %wheel ALL=(ALL)              ALL
  ```
  * **`test` / `%wheel`:** User or **group (prefixed with `%`)** granted privileges.
  * **`openeuler.com` / `ALL`:** Hostname where the rule applies.
  * **`(root)` / `(ALL)`:** Target user identity for privilege escalation.
  * **`NOPASSWD:/usr/bin/touch`:** Optional `NOPASSWD:` tag (skips password prompt) + comma-separated list of allowed absolute command paths.
* **Key `sudo` Options:** **`-l`** (list current user's allowed `sudo` permissions), **`-k`** (invalidate cached credentials, forcing password on next run), **`-v`** (extend password timeout by 5 mins), **`-u user/#uid`** (run as specific user), **`-b`** (run in background).
key_takeaways: When the Sticky Bit ('drwxrwxrwt') is set on a directory, only the file owner, directory owner, or root can delete or rename files inside it.
A '+' at the end of 'ls -l' permissions (-rw-rw-r--+) indicates an ACL is active; manage ACLs with getfacl, setfacl (-m modify, -x delete entry, -b remove all), and chacl.
su requires the target user's password and does not log commands; sudo requires the current user's password, checks /etc/sudoers (or /etc/sudoers.d/<user>), and logs all executed commands.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: 'su username' switches the user identity WITHOUT changing the current shell environment variables, whereas 'su - username' starts a full login shell with the target user's environment!
EXAM TRAP: In /etc/sudoers, a percent sign ('%') before a name (e.g., '%wheel') indicates a user group rather than an individual user.

lecture.title: RPM Package Management & DNF Repository Configuration (`rpm`, `createrepo`)
objectives: Parse the standard RPM package naming format (`name-version-release.arch.rpm`) and execute install, upgrade, uninstall, and query commands (`rpm`)
Explain why DNF ('next-generation YUM') outperforms YUM using `libsolv` and Python 3 plugins
Configure `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf`, `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` files, and local software repositories using `createrepo`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. RPM Package Naming & Core `rpm` Commands
* **RPM Naming Format:** `name-version-release.arch.rpm` (e.g., `iSulad-2.0.11-1.oe2203.aarch64.rpm`).
* **Installation, Upgrade & Removal:**
  * **`rpm -ivh example.rpm`:** Installs a package (`-i` install, `-v` verbose details, `-h` hash `#` progress bar).
  * **`rpm -Uvh example.rpm`:** Upgrades a package (replaces existing package, or **installs it if not yet installed**).
  * **`rpm -Fvh example.rpm`:** Freshens/upgrades **only if an earlier version is already installed**.
  * **`rpm -e example`:** Uninstalls a package. Force options: **`--nodeps`** (ignore dependencies—use with caution) and **`--allmatches`** (remove all versions); **`--force`** (forcibly install/overwrite files).
* **Query & Validation Options (`rpm -q...`):**
  * **`-q <pkg>`:** Checks if package is installed. **`-qa`:** Lists **all** installed RPM packages.
  * **`-qi <pkg>`:** Displays detailed package description/metadata (`-qpi` for an uninstalled `.rpm` file).
  * **`-ql <pkg>`:** Lists all files and full paths installed by the package (`-qpl` for an uninstalled `.rpm` file).
  * **`-qf <filepath>`:** Queries **which RPM package owns a specific file** on the server.
  * **`-qc <pkg>` / `-qd <pkg>`:** Lists **configuration files (`-qc`)** or **documentation files (`-qd`)**.
  * **`-Va`:** Validates all installed RPM packages to detect missing or modified files.

---

### 2. Evolution from YUM to DNF & `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf`
* **Why DNF?** RPM does not resolve dependencies automatically. **YUM** solved dependency management but suffered from high memory usage and slow dependency resolution on large trees. **DNF (Next-Generation YUM)** maintains CLI compatibility with YUM while using the **`libsolv`** library for fast dependency resolution, lower memory footprint, and a modern **Python 3** plugin architecture.
* **Global Config (`/etc/dnf/dnf.conf` — `[main]` section):**
  * **`cachedir`:** Directory storing downloaded RPMs and database cache.
  * **`best`:** Always attempts to install the latest available version (default: **`True`**).
  * **`installonly_limit`:** Max number of concurrent versions for `installonlypkgs` like kernels (default: **`3`**; do not decrease).
  * **`clean_requirements_on_remove`:** Automatically removes unused dependency packages during `dnf remove` (default: **`True`**).

---

### 3. Configuring `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` & Local Repositories
Repository files reside in **`/etc/yum.repos.d/`** by default:
```ini
[OS]
name=OS
baseurl=https://repo.openeuler.org/openEuler-24.03-LTS-SP1/OS/$basearch/
metalink=https://mirrors.openeuler.org/metalink?repo=releasever/OS&arch=basearch
metadata_expire=1h
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
gpgkey=http://repo.openeuler.org/openEuler-24.03-LTS-SP1/OS/$basearch/RPM-GPG-KEY-openEuler
```
* **`baseurl`** supports three protocols: `http://`, `ftp://`, and **`file:///`** (for local paths).
* **Creating a Local Repository (`createrepo`):**
  1. Install tool as root: `dnf install createrepo`
  2. Place RPM packages in `/mnt/local_repo/`
  3. Generate metadata database: **`createrepo --database /mnt/local_repo`**
key_takeaways: rpm -ivh installs, rpm -Uvh upgrades (or installs), rpm -Fvh upgrades only existing packages, rpm -e uninstalls, rpm -qf <file> finds which package owns a file, and rpm -qc lists config files.
DNF ('next-generation YUM') uses the libsolv library and Python 3 plugins; its global config is /etc/dnf/dnf.conf (default installonly_limit=3) and repo files live in /etc/yum.repos.d/.
To build a local repository from a folder of RPMs, install createrepo and run 'createrepo --database /mnt/local_repo'.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse /etc/dnf/dnf.conf (global DNF configuration) with /etc/yum.repos.d/ (default directory for .repo files)!
EXAM TRAP: To query files inside an UNINSTALLED .rpm package file on disk, you must include the '-p' flag (e.g., 'rpm -qpl pkg.rpm' or 'rpm -qilp pkg.rpm').

lecture.title: DNF Repository, Package & Package Group Management (`dnf`, `dnf config-manager`)
objectives: Add, list, enable, and disable repositories using `dnf config-manager` (`--add-repo`, `--set-enable`, `--set-disable`) and `dnf repolist`
Search, list, inspect, download (with dependencies), install, and remove RPM packages using `dnf`
Query, install, and remove software package groups (`dnf groups summary`, `dnf group list`, `dnf group install`, `dnf group remove`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Managing Repositories with `dnf config-manager` and `dnf repolist`
Only the **`root`** user can add, enable, or disable `.repo` files in `/etc/yum.repos.d/`:
* **Add a New Repository:**
  ```bash
  dnf config-manager --add-repo repository_url
  ```
  Automatically generates a corresponding `.repo` file inside `/etc/yum.repos.d/`.
* **View Repository IDs:**
  ```bash
  dnf repolist
  ```
* **Enable or Disable a Repository by ID:**
  ```bash
  dnf config-manager --set-enable repository_id
  dnf config-manager --set-disable repository_id
  ```

---

### 2. Searching, Listing, Downloading, Installing & Removing Packages
| Task | DNF Command Syntax & Key Options |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Search by keyword** | **`dnf search term`** (searches package names, abbreviations, and descriptions). |
| **List packages** | **`dnf list all`** (lists all installed and available packages) or **`dnf list glob_expression...`**. |
| **View package details** | **`dnf info package_name...`** |
| **Download RPMs** | **`dnf download package_name`**. To also download uninstalled dependencies, add **`--resolve`**: **`dnf download --resolve package_name`**. |
| **Install packages** | **`dnf install package_name`**. When installing multiple packages simultaneously (`dnf install pkg1 pkg2 --setopt=strict=0` or `strict=False` in `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf`), available packages are still installed even if one package name is unavailable. |
| **Remove packages** | **`dnf remove package_name...`** |

---

### 3. Managing Software Package Groups (`dnf group`)
A **package group** is a curated collection of related software packages (such as `System Tools` or `Development Tools`) identified by both a **group name** and a **group ID**:
* **View Summary of Installed & Available Groups:**
  ```bash
  dnf groups summary
  ```
* **List All Package Groups and Group IDs:**
  ```bash
  dnf group list
  ```
* **Install or Remove a Package Group:**
  ```bash
  dnf group install group_name/groupid
  dnf group remove group_name/groupid
  ```
key_takeaways: Use 'dnf config-manager --add-repo <url>' to add a repository in /etc/yum.repos.d/, 'dnf repolist' to check repo IDs, and '--set-enable' / '--set-disable' to toggle them.
Use 'dnf download --resolve <pkg>' to download an RPM package along with all its uninstalled dependency packages.
Use 'dnf groups summary' and 'dnf group list' to inspect software package groups, and 'dnf group install <name/id>' or 'dnf group remove <name/id>' to manage them.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Only the root user can add a .repo file or run 'dnf config-manager --add-repo' / '--set-enable' / '--set-disable'.

EXAM TRAP: When installing multiple packages at once with 'dnf install pkg1 pkg2', adding '--setopt=strict=0' (or setting 'strict=False' in /etc/dnf/dnf.conf) allows DNF to skip unavailable packages and continue installing valid ones.
