lecture.title: `systemd` Service Architecture, Unit Files & `journald` Log Management
objectives: Explain `systemd` (PID 1) advantages over SysVinit, its 3 invoked kernel modules (`cgroups`, `autofs`, `kdbus`), and its 12 Unit types
Parse the 3 sections of a `systemd` unit file (`[Unit]`, `[Service]`, `[Install]`) and key directives (`After=`, `Requires=`, `Wants=`, `ExecStart=`, `WantedBy=`)
Control service lifecycle with `systemctl` and query centralized service logs with `journalctl -u <service>`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. `systemd` Architecture (PID 1) & Unit Types * **What is `systemd`?** **`systemd`** is the **first system program (`PID 1`)** loaded by the Linux kernel at boot. Compared with legacy `SysVinit`, `systemd` provides fast parallel activation, on-demand activation, process lifecycle tracking via **cgroups**, mount/automount management, transactional dependency management, backwards compatibility with SysVinit scripts, and system snapshots/restoration. * **Three Kernel Modules Directly Invoked by `systemd` (Ch.04, p.217):** 1. **`cgroups`**: Resource control and restriction. 2. **`autofs`**: Automatic file system mounting. 3. **`kdbus`**: Kernel message passing. * **12 `systemd` Unit Types:** * **`service`** (system service), **`target`** (group of units / runlevel, e.g., `multi-user.target`, `graphical.target`), **`automount`**, **`device`**, **`mount`**, **`path`**, **`scope`** (externally created process), **`snapshot`**, **`slice`** (hierarchical cgroup process tree), **`socket`** (IPC socket), **`swap`**, and **`timer`**. --- ### 2. Anatomy of a `systemd` Unit File (3 Sections) A complete `.service` unit file consists of **three sections** (Ch.04, p.219): | Section | Key Directives & Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | **`[Unit]`** | Defines service metadata, startup order, and dependencies:
• **`Description=`**: Brief description shown in `systemctl status`.
• **`After=`**: Ordering rule—start this unit *after* the specified unit starts.
• **`Requires=`**: **Hard dependency**—startup fails if the required dependency is missing/fails.
• **`Wants=`**: **Soft dependency**—if the dependency is missing/fails, this service **can still start**. | | **`[Service]`** | Defines service execution behavior:
• **`ExecStart=` (Mandatory):** Command to start the service.
• **`ExecStop=`**: Command to stop the service.
• **`Restart=`**: Auto-restart policy (`always`, `on-failure`, etc.).
• **`User=`**: User account under which the service runs (`root` by default). | | **`[Install]`** | Defines how `systemctl enable` integrates the service into boot targets:
• **`WantedBy=`**: Target unit associated when enabled (e.g., `multi-user.target`). | --- ### 3. `systemctl` Operations & `journald` (`journalctl`) * **Service Lifecycle Commands (`systemctl`):** * **`systemctl start / stop / restart .service`** * **`systemctl enable / disable .service`** (enable/disable auto-start at boot) * **`systemctl list-units --type service`** (add **`-all`** to view all active and inactive services) * **`systemctl status .service`**: Displays `Loaded` (path & enabled state), `Active` (running status & timestamp), `Main PID`, `CGroup`, and recent log fragments. * **Centralized Log Management (`journald` & `journalctl`):** * `journald` is a subsystem of `systemd` that automatically records all service logs. * While `systemctl status ` shows only recent log fragments, **`journalctl -u `** displays the **complete service logs**!
key_takeaways: systemd is PID 1 and directly invokes 3 kernel modules: cgroups (resource control), autofs (auto-mounting), and kdbus (message passing).

A systemd unit file has 3 sections: [Unit] (Description, After, Requires [hard dependency], Wants [soft dependency]), [Service] (ExecStart [mandatory], ExecStop, Restart, User), and [Install] (WantedBy).
Use 'systemctl start/stop/restart/enable/disable/status <name>.service' to manage services, and 'journalctl -u <service>' to view complete service logs.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: In the [Unit] section, 'Requires=' declares a HARD dependency (service fails if dependency is missing), whereas 'Wants=' declares a SOFT dependency (service still starts if dependency is missing)!
EXAM TRAP: 'systemctl status <service>' displays only service log fragments; use 'journalctl -u <service>' to display complete service logs.

lecture.title: Process Management (`ps`, `top`, `nice`, `kill`) & Scheduled Tasks (`at`, `crontab`)
objectives: Explain the 5 Linux process memory segments, Copy-on-Write (`fork`/`exec`/`exit`/`wait`) lifecycle, and 5 kernel process states
Monitor and control processes with `ps`, `top` (dynamically checks host resource usage — Ch.04 Quiz!), `nice`/`renice` (`PRI` vs. `NI`), `&`/`jobs`/`fg`/`bg`, and `kill`/`killall` signals
Schedule one-time tasks with `at` (`atq`, `atrm`) and recurring periodic tasks with `crontab` (5-field syntax `min hour dom month dow`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Process Memory, Lifecycle & States
* **5 Virtual Address Space Segments (Low to High Address):** **Code segment** (read-only executable code/constants) -> **Data segment** (initialized static/global variables) -> **BSS segment** (uninitialized static/global variables) -> **Heap** (dynamic memory) -> **Stack** (local variables).
* **Lifecycle & Copy-on-Write (COW):** Parent calls **`fork()`** (shares address space via COW) -> Child calls **`exec()`** (loads new program; kernel allocates new physical pages on write) -> Child calls **`exit()`** and becomes a **Zombie process** until the parent reaps it via **`wait()`**.
* **5 Process States (Ch.04, p.227):**
  * **`TASK_RUNNING` (`running/0`):** Running in user/kernel space or ready in the run queue.
  * **`TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE` (`interruptible/1`):** Sleeping; can be woken by resources, signals, or clock interrupts.
  * **`TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE` (`uninterruptible/2`):** Sleeping on hardware I/O; **cannot** be woken by signals.
  * **`TASK_ZOMBIE` (`zombie/3`):** Terminated, but process control block (PCB) is not yet released by parent `wait()`.
  * **`TASK_STOPPED` (`stopped/4`):** Stopped (e.g., by debugger or `SIGSTOP`/`SIGTSTP`).

---

### 2. Priority (`PRI`/`NI`), Monitoring (`ps`/`top`), Job Control & Signals
* **Priority (`PRI` vs. `NI`):** Internal kernel priority is **`0–139`** (`0–99` real-time, `100–139` non-real-time; **smaller value = higher priority**). **`NI` (nice value)** ranges from **`-20` (highest priority)** to **`19` (lowest priority)** (default `0`). Formula: **`PRI(new) = PRI(old) + nice`**. Only **`root`** can set a negative `nice` value!
  * Launch with nice: `nice -n -18 vi &`
  * Modify running process: `renice -n 12 -p 9700` (supports `-p` PID, `-g` group, `-u` user; or press `r` inside `top`).
* **Static vs. Dynamic Monitoring (Official Ch.04 Quiz Q1!):**
  * **`ps aux` / `ps -ef` / `ps -l`:** **Statically** lists process snapshot at a single point in time.
  * **`top`:** **Dynamically checks host resource usage and processes in real time** (Ch.04 Quiz Q1!).
* **Foreground/Background & Signals (`kill` / `killall`):**
  * **`&`** (run in background), **`Ctrl+Z`** (suspend foreground job to background), **`jobs`** (list background jobs), **`fg`** (bring to foreground), **`bg`** (resume in background).
  * **Key Signals:** **`1` (`HUP` - Hangup/reload)**, **`2` (`INT` - `Ctrl+C` interrupt)**, **`3` (`QUIT`)**, **`9` (`KILL` - unconditional termination)**, **`11` (`SEGV` - segment error)**, **`15` (`TERM` - default termination signal of `kill PID`)**, **`17` (`STOP`)**, **`18` (`TSTP` - `Ctrl+Z`)**, **`19` (`CONT` - continue)**. Note: `killall python*` supports wildcards by process name!

---

### 3. Scheduled Tasks: One-Time (`at`) vs. Periodic (`cron` / `crontab`)
* **One-Time Task (`at` — managed by `atd` daemon checking `/var/spool/at`):**
  * Controlled by `/etc/at.allow` and `/etc/at.deny`.
  * Interactive: `at 16:30` -> enter commands -> press **`Ctrl+D`** to submit; or script file: **`at -f example.sh 15:00`**.
  * Relative time examples: `at now+4 hours`, `at now+240 minutes`, `at 4:30pm`, `at teatime` (`16:00`).
  * Queue inspection & removal: **`atq`** (view job queue) and **`atrm <job_ID>`** (delete job).
* **Periodic Task (`cron` — wakes up every minute to read `/var/spool/cron/<user>` and `/etc/crontab`):**
  * Commands: **`crontab -e`** (edit), **`crontab -l`** (list), **`crontab -r`** (remove), **`crontab -u <user>`** (root only). **No need to restart `crond` after editing!**
  * **5 Time Fields:** `minute(0-59)  hour(0-23)  day-of-month(1-31)  month-of-year(1-12)  day-of-week(0-6, 0=Sunday)  command`
  * Special symbols: **`*`** (all values), **`/`** (step, e.g., `*/5`), **`-`** (range), **`,`** (discrete list). Example: `00 08 * * 1 commands` (every Monday at 08:00 AM). In `/etc/crontab`, **`run-parts`** executes all scripts inside a directory (`/etc/cron.hourly`, `/etc/cron.daily`, etc.).
key_takeaways: top dynamically checks host resource usage in real time (Ch.04 Quiz Q1), whereas ps lists a static snapshot.

PRI(new) = PRI(old) + nice, where nice ranges from -20 (highest priority, root only) to 19 (lowest priority); kill sends signal 15 (TERM) by default, while signal 9 (KILL) forces unconditional termination.

at schedules one-time tasks (atq lists, atrm deletes, Ctrl+D ends interactive input); crontab (-e/-l/-r/-u) schedules periodic tasks using 'minute hour day-of-month month-of-year day-of-week command'.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Official Ch.04 Quiz Q1): 'Which of the following commands can be used to dynamically check the host resource usage?' -> B. top (ps, free, and lscpu are static snapshots)!
EXAM TRAP: Do NOT restart the cron service after modifying a crontab file—the cron daemon wakes up every minute and automatically re-reads /etc/crontab and /var/spool/cron (Ch.04 p.247)!

lecture.title: Persistent Storage, File Systems & Disk Partitioning (`fdisk`, `parted`, MBR vs. GPT)
objectives: Identify the 3 persistent storage layers, openEuler's default file system (`ext4`), and commands to view file system/disk info (`lsblk -f`, `blkid`, `df -T`, `fdisk -l`, `df -h`)
Decode Linux disk and partition device names (`/dev/xxyN`) across IDE (`hd`), SCSI/SATA/SAS/SSD (`sd`), and virtio (`vd`) drives
Compare MBR vs. GPT partitioning limits and partition drives using `fdisk` and `parted`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Persistent Storage Layers, File Systems & Disk Inspection
* **3 Layers of Linux Persistent Storage:** (1) **File system** (organizes/manages file data), (2) **Disk partitions** (logical sections), (3) **Physical drives** (HDD, SSD, NVMe).
* **File Systems on openEuler:**
  * **Default file system on openEuler:** **`ext4`** (Ch.05, p.259).
  * Other supported file systems: **XFS** (high-performance journaling FS by Silicon Graphics, excels at large files), **VFAT** (DOS/Windows FAT16/FAT32), **NFS** (UNIX network file sharing), **ISO 9660** (optical discs/ISOs), **Btrfs**, etc.
  * **Check File System Type:** **`lsblk -f`**, **`blkid`**, or **`df -T`**.
  * **Check Disk & Mount Space:** **`fdisk -l`** (lists all mounted and unmounted disks/partitions) and **`df -h`** (checks mounted disk space and usage).
* **Disk Interfaces:** **IDE (PATA / parallel port)**, **SATA (serial port)**, **SCSI / SAS** (server-grade, hot-swappable, high stability), and **Fibre Channel (FC)**.

---

### 2. Device Naming (`/dev/xxyN`) & Partition Types
In `/dev/xxyN`:
* **`xx` (Device Type):** **`hd`** (IDE disk), **`sd`** (SCSI, SAS, SATA, and SSD disks), **`vd`** (virtio virtual disk), **`fd`** (floppy disk).
* **`y` (Device Letter):** `a` = 1st disk, `b` = 2nd disk (e.g., `/dev/hda` = 1st IDE disk, `/dev/sdb` = 2nd SCSI/SATA disk).
* **`N` (Partition Number):**
  * **`1 to 4`:** Reserved for **Primary partitions** or the **Extended partition** (at most **1 extended partition** per disk, which cannot be used directly until divided into logical partitions).
  * **`5 and above`:** **Logical partitions ALWAYS start from 5!** Example: **`/dev/sdb6` is the second logical partition on the second SCSI disk**!

---

### 3. MBR (`fdisk`) vs. GPT (`parted`)
| Feature | MBR (Master Boot Record — `fdisk`) | GPT (GUID Partition Table — `parted`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Firmware & Address Bits** | Legacy **BIOS**; **32-bit** sector values. | **UEFI** standard; **64-bit** LBA values. |
| **Max Disk/Partition Size** | **2 TB** maximum (`fdisk` does not support >2 TB). | **18 EB** maximum (supports >2 TB). |
| **Max Partitions** | **4 primary** (or 3 primary + 1 extended). Total usable: **SCSI max 15** (4 primary or 12 logical); **IDE max 63** (4 primary or 60 logical). | **128 partitions** per disk (no primary/extended/logical distinction). |
| **Interactive Commands** | `fdisk /dev/sdb`: **`n`** (new: `p` primary, `e` extended, `l` logical), **`d`** (delete), **`p`** (print table), **`l`** (list IDs: `82` swap, `83` Linux, **`8e` Linux LVM**), **`t`** (change ID), **`w`** (save & exit), **`q`** (quit without saving). | `parted /dev/sdb`: **`mklabel gpt`** (set GPT table), **`mkpart`** (create partition), **`print`**, **`resizepart`**, **`rm`**, **`quit`**. Non-interactive: `parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt` -> `parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary 0 1000`. |
key_takeaways: The default file system on openEuler is ext4; check file system types using 'lsblk -f', 'blkid', or 'df -T'.
In /dev/xxyN, partitions 1–4 are primary or extended partitions, and logical partitions ALWAYS start at 5 (so /dev/sdb6 is the 2nd logical partition on the 2nd SCSI disk).
MBR (fdisk) is limited to 2 TB and 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended), whereas GPT (parted) supports up to 18 EB and 128 partitions.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Even if you create only 1 primary partition (/dev/sdb1) and 1 extended partition (/dev/sdb2), the very first logical partition inside that extended partition is ALWAYS numbered 5 (/dev/sdb5), and the second logical partition is /dev/sdb6!
EXAM TRAP: In fdisk, partition ID '83' is standard Linux, '82' is Linux swap, and '8e' is Linux LVM (must change 83 to 8e using 't' when preparing a partition for LVM).

lecture.title: Drive Formatting (`mkfs`), Mounting (`mount`/`umount`) & `/etc/fstab` Persistence
objectives: Format partitions using `mkfs -t ext4 <device>` (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q2!) or `mkfs.ext4` and understand `mkfs` options (`-V`, `-t`, `-c`, `-l`)
Distinguish temporary mounting (`mount <device> <dir>`) vs. permanent boot-time mounting via `/etc/fstab`
Configure all 6 fields of `/etc/fstab` (`<file system> <dir> <type> <options> <dump> <pass>`) and fsck `pass` priorities (`0`, `1`, `2`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Drive Formatting with `mkfs`
Formatting initializes a partition with a file system structure (deleting existing data on that partition).
* **Viewing Supported File System Formatters:** Type `mkfs` and press **`Tab` twice** to list all `mkfs.*` utilities (`mkfs.ext4`, `mkfs.xfs`, `mkfs.vfat`, etc.).
* **Syntax & Equivalent Forms (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q2!):**
  ```bash
  mkfs [-V] [-t fstype] [fs-options] filesys [blocks]
  # Example 1 (Ch.05 Quiz Q2 exact answer):
  mkfs -t ext4 /dev/hdb6
  # Example 2:
  mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb2
  ```
* **Key `mkfs` Options (Ch.05, p.279):**
  * **`-t <fstype>`:** Specifies the file system type to build. (**Note:** If `-t` is omitted in plain `mkfs`, the default value for Linux is **`ext2`**!).
  * **`-c`:** Checks the partition for **bad blocks** before building the file system.
  * **`-l bad_blocks_file`:** Reads bad block information from `bad_blocks_file`.
  * **`-V`:** Produces verbose output.

---

### 2. Temporary Mounting (`mount`) vs. Permanent Mounting (`/etc/fstab`)
Because Linux follows the *"Everything is a file"* design, a formatted partition must be linked to a directory (**mount point**, such as `/mnt`, `/media`, or a custom directory) before it can be accessed:
* **Temporary Mounting:**
  ```bash
  mount /dev/sda5 /test
  ```
  Mounts `/dev/sda5` to `/test` immediately, **but becomes invalid after the system is restarted!**
* **Permanent Mounting (`/etc/fstab`):**
  The OS automatically reads **`/etc/fstab`** at boot (or when **`mount -a`** is run) and mounts all listed file systems.

---

### 3. The 6 Fields of `/etc/fstab`
```text
<file system>   <dir>   <type>   <options>           <dump>  <pass>
tmpfs           /tmp    tmpfs    nodev,nosuid        0       0
/dev/sda1       /       ext4     defaults,noatime    0       1
/dev/sda2       none    swap     defaults            0       0
```
1. **`<file system>`:** Device path (`/dev/sda1`) or `UUID=...` (from `blkid`).
2. **`<dir>`:** Mount point directory (`/` or `none` for `swap`).
3. **`<type>`:** File system type (`ext4`, `xfs`, `swap`, `tmpfs`).
4. **`<options>`:** Mount parameters: **`defaults`**, **`auto`** (mounts at boot or `mount -a`), **`ro`** / **`rw`**, **`user`** / **`nouser`**, **`dev`** / **`nodev`**, **`suid`** / **`nosuid`**, **`sync`** / **`async`**, **`noatime`** / **`nodiratime`** (skips updating inode access times to improve performance).
5. **`<dump>`:** Backup flag (`0` = do not back up with `dump` [recommended]; `1` = back up).
6. **`<pass>` (`fsck` check priority):**
   * **`0`**: Device is **not checked** by `fsck`.
   * **`1`**: **Root partition (`/`)** — checked first!
   * **`2`**: **Other devices** that need to be checked after root.
key_takeaways: Format a partition into ext4 using 'mkfs -t ext4 /dev/hdb6' (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q2) or 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/hdb6'; there is NO 'format' or 'makefile' command in Linux!
Mounting with 'mount /dev/sda5 /test' is temporary and lost on reboot; configure permanent mounting in /etc/fstab.
The 6 fields of /etc/fstab are: <file system> <dir> <type> <options> <dump> <pass>, where <pass> is 1 for root (/), 2 for other checked partitions, and 0 for no fsck check.

Execute online LV capacity expansion (`lvextend` + `resize2fs`) and safe offline LV capacity reduction (`umount` -> `e2fsck -f` -> `resize2fs` -> `lvreduce` -> `mount`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. LVM Architecture & Core Components
**Logical Volume Management (LVM)** is a logical storage layer built **above physical disks/partitions and below file systems**, enabling dynamic capacity expansion/reduction, disk striping, mirroring, and snapshots.

| Component | Definition & Key Rules (Ch.05, pp. 284–285) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **PV (Physical Volume)** | Underlying physical drive (`/dev/sdd`) or partition (`/dev/sdb1`, partition ID changed from `83` to **`8e`** in `fdisk`). |
| **VG (Volume Group)** | Storage pool combining **one or more PVs** (`VG` shields underlying PV boundaries). |
| **PE (Physical Extent)** | **Smallest unit that can be addressed by LVM.** Default size is **4 MB**. **Once a VG's PE size is determined (`vgcreate -s`), it CANNOT be changed**, and all PVs in the same VG share the same PE size. |
| **LE (Logical Extent)** | **Minimum storage unit that can be allocated** in LVM. In the same VG, **LE size = PE size** (1:1 correspondence). |
| **LV (Logical Volume)** | Logical partition carved out of a VG, formatted with `mkfs` and mounted for end users. |

---

### 2. LVM Creation & Management Commands
1. **PV Commands:**
   * Create: **`pvcreate /dev/hda{6,7,8,9}`** (options: `-f` force, `-u` UUID, `-y` answer yes).
   * Inspect/Manage: **`pvs`** (concise overview), **`pvdisplay`** (detailed), **`pvscan`**, **`pvchange`**, **`pvresize`**, **`pvremove`**, **`pvmove`**, **`pvck`**.
2. **VG Commands:**
   * Create: **`vgcreate [-l max_LV] [-p max_PV] [-s PE_size] vg1000 /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdb2`**
   * Inspect/Manage: **`vgs`**, **`vgdisplay`**, **`vgscan`**, **`vgextend`** (add PVs to VG), **`vgreduce`** (remove PV from VG after moving data), **`vgremove`**, **`vgrename`**, **`vgchange`**, **`vgcfgbackup`**, **`vgcfgrestore`**, **`vgimport`**, **`vgexport`**.
3. **LV Commands:**
   * Create: **`lvcreate -L 200M [-n lvname] vg1000`** (`-L` specifies size in K/M/G/T; **`-l`** specifies number of **LEs**; **`-s`** creates a snapshot).
   * Inspect/Manage: **`lvs`**, **`lvdisplay [-m]`**, **`lvscan`**, **`lvextend [--resizefs]`**, **`lvreduce`**, **`lvresize`**, **`lvremove`**, **`lvrename`**, **`lvconvert`**.

---

### 3. Expanding vs. Reducing LV Capacity (High-Yield Exam Workflows!)
* **Expanding LV Capacity (Supports ONLINE expansion without unmounting! — Ch.05, p.298):**
  1. Run **`vgs`** to check if the VG has sufficient free space (if not, run `vgextend`).
  2. Expand the LV: **`lvextend -L +SIZE lv_device`** (or `lvresize -L +200M /dev/vg1000/lvol0`).
  3. Resize the `ext4` file system online: **`resize2fs device`** (or use `lvextend --resizefs` in newer versions).
* **Reducing LV Capacity (Risky — MUST unmount and shrink file system FIRST! — Ch.05, p.299):**
  1. Determine target size and verify enough space for existing data.
  2. Unmount the file system (**`umount`**) and run a forcible check (**`e2fsck -f device`**).
  3. **Shrink the file system first:** **`resize2fs device TARGET_SIZE`**.
  4. **Shrink the LV second:** **`lvreduce -L TARGET_SIZE lv_device`**.
  5. **Mount** the file system again (**`mount`**).
key_takeaways: The default Physical Extent (PE) size in LVM is 4 MB; once set during vgcreate, a VG's PE size cannot be changed, and LE size equals PE size within the same VG.
In lvcreate/lvresize, uppercase '-L' specifies capacity in bytes (K/M/G/T), whereas lowercase '-l' specifies the number of Logical Extents (LEs).
LV expansion can be done ONLINE without unmounting (vgs -> lvextend -> resize2fs), whereas LV reduction MUST be done OFFLINE in strict order: umount -> e2fsck -f -> resize2fs -> lvreduce -> mount.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Never run 'lvreduce' BEFORE 'resize2fs'! When expanding, you expand the LV first (lvextend) and the file system second (resize2fs); when reducing, you MUST unmount, check (e2fsck -f), shrink the file system first (resize2fs), and shrink the LV second (lvreduce)!
EXAM TRAP: When using fdisk to create a partition for LVM, the default partition ID is 83 (Linux); change it to 8e (Linux LVM) before running pvcreate.

lecture.title: openEuler Network Configuration (`ip`, `nmcli`, `nmtui`, `ifcfg`) & Diagnosis (`ping`, `tracepath`, `ss`)
objectives: Query IP addresses, routes, DNS, and hostnames (`ip addr`, `ifconfig`, `ip route show`, `route -n` [temporary — Ch.05 Quiz Q1!], `/etc/resolv.conf`, `hostnamectl`)
Decode Predictable Network Interface Names (`en`, `wl`, `ww` + `p`, `o`, `s`, `x`, `u`) and legacy `/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-*` files
Configure connections and static routes with `nmcli` and `nmtui`, and diagnose networks with `ping`, `tracepath`, and `ss`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Querying Network State, Routes & Hostnames
* **Viewing IP, Gateway & DNS:**
  * **IP & Mask:** **`ip addr`** or **`ifconfig`**.
  * **Gateway & Routing Table:** **`ip route show`** or **`route -n`**.
  * **Official Ch.05 Quiz Q1 Rule:** The **`route`** command can view or configure host route information, **but routes configured via the `route` command are TEMPORARY and do NOT remain valid permanently after a reboot!**
  * **DNS Server:** **`cat /etc/resolv.conf`** (generated by NetworkManager; `nameserver <IP>`).
* **Setting the System Hostname (3 Methods — Ch.05, p.305):**
  1. **Temporary (until next restart):** **`hostname new-name`**
  2. **Permanent (CLI):** **`hostnamectl set-hostname new-name`** (or via `nmtui`)
  3. **Permanent (Config file):** Write the new name to **`/etc/hostname`**.

---

### 2. Predictable NIC Naming Rules & `ifcfg-*` Files
openEuler uses `systemd/udev` **Predictable Network Interface Names** (e.g., **`enp0s3`**, **`wlp3s0`**; falls back to **`eth0`** if rules cannot be applied):
* **2-Letter Type Prefix:** **`en`** (Ethernet), **`wl`** (Wireless LAN / Wi-Fi), **`ww`** (WWAN).
* **Location/Hardware Scheme:**
  * **`p<bus>s<slot>`**: PCIe slot (`p0s3`).
  * **`o<index>`**: Onboard integrated NIC (`o1`).
  * **`s<slot>[f<func>]`**: Hot-swappable slot / SR-IOV virtual function (`s0f1`).
  * **`x<MAC>`**: MAC address-based (`x78e7d1`).
  * **`u<port>`**: USB device port (`u2`).
* **Config Files (`/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-*`):** Key parameters: `TYPE`, `BOOTPROTO` (`dhcp`/`static`/`none`), `ONBOOT` (`yes`/`no`), `IPADDR`, `NETMASK`, `GATEWAY`, `BROADCAST`, `HWADDR`/`MACADDR`, `PEERDNS`, `DNS1`/`DNS2`, `USERCTL`, `NAME`, `DEVICE`. *(Note: In kernel 3.x+, Huawei recommends **`nmcli`** or **`nmtui`** over manual `ifcfg-*` editing).*

---

### 3. NetworkManager (`nmcli` & `nmtui`) and Network Diagnosis (`ping`, `tracepath`, `ss`)
* **Device vs. Connection:** A **Device** is a physical/virtual NIC (`enp4s0`); a **Connection** is a configuration profile. **A device can have multiple connections, but only ONE connection can be active on a device at a time!**
* **`nmcli` Core Commands:**
  * Show connections: **`nmcli connection show [--active]`**
  * Add DHCP connection: **`nmcli connection add con-name 'Demo' type Ethernet ifname enp4s0`**
  * Add Static IP connection: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name my-eth ifname eth0 ip4 192.168.1.100/24 gw4 192.168.1.1`
  * Modify DNS / Add secondary DNS (`+`/`-`): **`nmcli con mod 'Demo' ipv4.dns 192.168.100.250`** and **`nmcli con mod "Euler" +ipv4.dns 114.114.114.114`**
  * Configure Static Route: **`nmcli connection modify enp3s0 +ipv4.routes "192.168.122.0/24 10.10.10.1"`** (or interactive `nmcli con edit`)
  * Activate connection (required for modifications to take effect!): **`nmcli connection up 'Demo'`**
* **`nmtui`:** Text-based curses GUI with 3 main actions: *Edit a connection*, *Activate a connection*, *Set system hostname*.
* **Network Diagnosis Utilities:**
  * **`ping`**: Sends **ICMP echo request** packets and waits for echo replies to test connectivity.
  * **`tracepath`**: Traces packet path from source to destination: (1) hop count/routing nodes, (2) RTT of each hop, (3) **detects Path MTU (`pmtu`) changes**.
  * **`ss` (Socket Statistics, e.g., `ss -talnp`)**: Displays network sockets/listening ports; **works faster than `netstat` by accessing data directly from the kernel!**
key_takeaways: Routes configured with the 'route' command are temporary and NOT permanent (Ch.05 Quiz Q1); use 'nmcli connection modify <con> +ipv4.routes "<subnet> <gw>"' for persistent static routes.
In NetworkManager, a device (NIC) can have multiple connections (profiles), but only ONE connection can be active at a time; run 'nmcli con up <name>' after modifying a connection.
tracepath measures hop count, per-hop RTT, and Path MTU (pmtu); ss (-talnp) is faster than netstat because it queries socket data directly from the kernel.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q1): '(True or false) The route command can view or configure host route information. Configured route information will remain valid permanently.' -> False (F)!
EXAM TRAP: 'hostname new-name' only changes the hostname temporarily until reboot; use 'hostnamectl set-hostname new-name' or edit '/etc/hostname' for a permanent change.

lecture.title: Shell Basics, Script Execution (`nohup`), Text Streams, Redirection & Pipes
objectives: Trace the history of Unix/Linux shells (V6 shell, sh, csh, tcsh, ksh, bash) and inspect shells via `/etc/shells`, `SHELL`, and `0`
Execute scripts via `sh script.sh`, `./script.sh` (`chmod +x`), `$PATH`, and persistent background mode (`nohup ./my_script.sh &`)
Redirect standard input/output/error streams (`>`, `>>`, `<`, `<< EOF`) and chain processes with IPC pipes (`|`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Shell Evolution & Inspecting Shells in openEuler
The **Shell** is the command interpreter in user space that parses user commands, expands variables, and invokes the Linux kernel.
* **Milestones in Shell History (Ch.06, p.327):**
  * **1971:** **Ken Thompson** (Bell Labs) develops the first Unix shell (**V6 shell**).
  * **1977:** **Steven Bourne** (Bell Labs) creates the **Bourne shell (`sh`)** for Unix V7.
  * **1978:** **Bill Joy** (UC Berkeley) develops the **C shell (`csh`)** for BSD.
  * **1983:** **Ken Greer** (CMU) develops **`tcsh`**; **David Korn** (Bell Labs) creates **KornShell (`ksh`)**.
  * **1989:** **Brian Fox** (GNU Project) develops the **Bourne Again Shell (`bash`)**, compatible with `sh`, `csh`, and `ksh`, and the **default shell of Linux/openEuler**.
* **Inspecting Shells (Ch.06, p.328):**
  * View all installed shells in the system: **`cat /etc/shells`**
  * View default shell of the current login user: **`echo $SHELL`**
  * View the currently running shell: **`echo $0`**

---

### 2. Specifying an Interpreter (`#!`) & Running Shell Scripts
* **Shebang (`#!`):** The first line of a script specifies the interpreter, e.g., **`#!/bin/bash`** or `#!/bin/csh`.
* **Execution Modes:**
  1. **`sh script_name.sh`:** Invokes the interpreter directly (does not require `x` permission on the file).
  2. **`./script_name.sh` (or via `PATH`):** Requires execute permission (**`chmod +x script_name.sh`**). To invoke by name from any directory, add its directory to `PATH` (persist by adding `export PATH="$PATH:/new/path"` to `.bashrc` or `.bash_profile`).
* **Background Execution (`&` vs. `nohup` — Ch.06, p.336):**
  * **`./my_script.sh &`:** Runs in the background, **but stops if you exit the shell!**
  * **`nohup ./my_script.sh &`:** Keeps the script running even after exiting the shell! Standard output and standard error are automatically redirected to **`nohup.out`**. View background jobs with **`jobs`**.

---

### 3. Text Streams, Redirection (`>`, `>>`, `<`, `<<`) & Pipes (`|`)
Every Linux process opens **three text stream interfaces**: **Standard Input (stdin)**, **Standard Output (stdout)**, and **Standard Error (stderr)**.
* **Output Redirection:**
  * **`ls > dir_log`:** Redirects stdout to `dir_log`, **overwriting** previous contents.
  * **`ls >> dir_log`:** Redirects stdout to `dir_log`, **appending** to the end of the file.
* **Input Redirection:**
  * **`command < inputfile`:** Uses `inputfile` as standard input (e.g., `wc -l < /dev/null`).
  * **`command << marker` (Inline Input Redirection / Here-Document):** Uses instant inline text as standard input until `marker` (commonly **`EOF`**) is encountered (`command << EOF > file`).
* **Pipe (`|`):** Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanism that connects the `stdout` of `command1` directly to the `stdin` of `command2` (`ls /bin/ | grep python | less`).
key_takeaways: Check installed shells with 'cat /etc/shells', default login shell with 'echo SHELL', and current shell with 'echo 0'.
Running './my_script.sh &' stops when the shell exits, whereas 'nohup ./my_script.sh &' keeps running after logout and redirects stdout/stderr to nohup.out.
'>' overwrites a file, '>>' appends to a file, '<' redirects file input, '<< EOF' provides inline input redirection (Here-Document), and '|' is an IPC pipe.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Running './script.sh' on a newly created file fails with 'Permission denied' unless you first grant execute permission with 'chmod +x script.sh' (or run it via 'sh script.sh').
EXAM TRAP: In inline input redirection ('command << EOF'), the marker 'EOF' marks the start and end of standard input and is NOT included in the standard input content itself!

lecture.title: Shell Variables, Quoting, `read` & Arithmetic Operations (`$[...]`, `++i` vs. `i++`)
objectives: Distinguish special characters (`#`, `'`, `\`, `/`, `!`), environment vs. user-defined variables, and `printenv` vs. `set`
Apply strict variable assignment rules (`variable=value` — NO spaces, `name==Tom` is FALSE [Ch.06 Quiz Q2!]), single vs. double quotes, `${VAR}` brace expansion, and `read`
Evaluate integer arithmetic using `$[expression]` (`*` = Multiplication [Ch.06 Quiz Q1!], operator precedence, and `++i` vs. `i++`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Special Characters & Variable Scopes (`printenv` vs. `set`)
* **5 Key Shell Special Characters (Ch.06, p.343):**
  * **`#` (Hashtag/Remarks):** Comments out lines (`#!` is shebang; `#` inside `'...'` or `"..."` is a literal `#`, not a comment!).
  * **`'` (Single Quote / Full Quoting):** Preserves the **exact literal value** of every character inside; **does NOT expand variables or commands**.
  * **`"` (Double Quote):** **Expands variables (`$VAR`) and commands** inside the quotes.
  * **`\` (Backslash / Escape):** Removes special meaning from the next character, or escapes a newline at the end of a line for line continuation.
  * **`/` (Forward Slash):** Root directory / path separator, or **division** in arithmetic (`a=4/2`).
  * **`!` (Bang / Negation):** Negates a test/exit status, `!=` (not equal), or character range negation (`ls a[!0-9]`).
* **Variable Types & Inspection (Ch.06, p.345):**
  * **Environment vs. User-defined**, scoped as **Global** (current shell + subshells; persisted via `export` in `.bash_profile` or `.bashrc`) or **Local**.
  * **`printenv` (or `env`):** Views **global environment variables**.
  * **`set`:** Built-in shell command that displays **ALL variables in a process** (local, global, user-defined, and shell functions).

---

### 2. Variable Naming, Assignment, Brace Expansion & `read`
* **Naming Rules:** Consists of letters, digits, and underscores (`_`); **must start with a letter or underscore (`_`)**; cannot use shell keywords.
* **Assignment Rule (Official Ch.06 Quiz Q2!):**
  * Syntax: **`variable=value`** (e.g., `name=Tom`).
  * **NO spaces are allowed on the left or right of `=`!**
  * **Official Ch.06 Quiz Q2 Trap:** *"An administrator can run the `name==Tom` command to assign value Tom to variable name."* -> **False!** (`==` is equality comparison, NOT assignment!).
* **Brace Expansion (`${VAR}` — Ch.06, p.347):**
  * If `FIRST=john`, `FIRST_=Jane`, and `LAST=Doe`, then `echo FIRST_LAST` outputs **`Doe`** (because bash looks up `FIRST_` + `LAST`? Wait: if `FIRST_` was unset it would output `Doe`; on Slide 27, when you want `FIRST` followed by `_` and `LAST`, you **must use braces**: **`echo ${FIRST}_$LAST` -> `john_Doe`**!).
* **`read <var>`:** Waits for user keyboard input and assigns it to `<var>`.

---

### 3. Arithmetic Operations (`$[...]`), Precedence & `++i` vs. `i++`
* **Syntax:** **`[expression]`** (e.g., `echo [1+1]` -> `2`, `echo $[2*2]` -> `4`).
* **Official Ch.06 Quiz Q1:** In a shell script arithmetic expression, **`*` means Multiplication**!
* **Arithmetic Operator Precedence (Highest to Lowest — Ch.06, p.352):**
  1. **`<VAR>++`, `<VAR>--`** (Post-increment / Post-decrement)
  2. **`++<VAR>`, `--<VAR>`** (Pre-increment / Pre-decrement)
  3. **`-`, `+`** (Unary minus / plus)
  4. **`**`** (Exponentiation)
  5. **`*`, `/`, `%`** (Multiplication, Division, Remainder)
  6. **`+`, `-`** (Addition, Subtraction)
* **`++i` vs. `i++` (Ch.06, p.353):**
  * `i++` creates a temporary variable to save the old value of `i`, returns that old value, and then increments `i` by 1.
  * `++i` directly adds 1 to `i`'s memory space and returns the new value without creating temporary space (higher performance).
  * **Slide 33 Example:** If `i=3`, `echo [++i]` outputs **`4`** (`i` becomes 4); then `echo [i++]` outputs **`4`** (returns old value 4, while `i` becomes 5); then `echo $i` outputs **`5`**!
key_takeaways: Variable assignment is 'variable=value' with NO spaces around '='; 'name==Tom' is NOT a valid assignment (Ch.06 Quiz Q2 = False).
Single quotes ('') preserve literal characters without variable expansion, whereas double quotes ("") expand variables and commands; use ${FIRST}_$LAST to disambiguate variable boundaries.
In a shell arithmetic expression ($[...]), '*' means Multiplication (Ch.06 Quiz Q1); printenv displays global variables, whereas 'set' displays all local, global, and user-defined variables.

EXAM TRAP (Official Ch.06 Quiz Q2): 'An administrator can run the name==Tom command to assign value Tom to variable name.' -> False!

lecture.title: Shell Conditional Statements (`if-then-elif-else-fi` and `case-in-esac`)
objectives: Explain how Bash `if` evaluates command exit status codes (`0` = True/Success, non-zero = False)
Write `if-then-fi`, `if-then-else-fi`, and `elif` conditional blocks using numeric, string, and file tests
Construct multi-branch `case ... in ... esac` statements using `|` pattern alternation, `;;` terminators, and `*` default wildcards
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. How `if-then-fi` Works in Bash (Exit Status Code `0`)
Unlike C or Java (where `if` evaluates a boolean `true`/`false` expression), **the Bash `if` statement executes the command following `if` and checks its exit status code (`$?`)**:
* **If the exit status code is `0` (Success):** Bash executes the commands inside the **`then`** block!
* **If the exit status code is non-zero (Failure):** Bash skips the `then` block (and evaluates `elif` / `else`, or moves to the next statement after `fi`).

```bash
if command
then
    commands
fi
```
* **Common Test Conditions (`[ ... ]` / `test` / `(( ... ))`):**
  * **Numeric comparisons:** `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-gt` (greater than), `-ge` (greater or equal), `-lt` (less than), `-le` (less or equal), or C-style `(( i % 5 == 0 ))`.
  * **String comparisons:** `=` / `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `-z` (empty string), `-n` (non-empty string).
  * **File checks:** `-e` (exists), `-f` (regular file), `-d` (directory), `-r` (readable), `-w` (writable), `-x` (executable).

---

### 2. Multi-Branch Judgment with `case ... in ... esac`
When checking a single variable against multiple distinct values/patterns, a **`case`** statement is cleaner and more readable than deeply nested `if-then-elif-else` blocks (Ch.06, p.357):

```bash
case variable in
pattern1 | pattern2)
    commands1
    ;;
pattern3)
    commands2
    ;;
*)
    default commands
    ;;
esac
```

---

### 3. Key Syntax Rules for `case` Statements
* **Opening & Closing Keywords:** Starts with **`case variable in`** and closes with **`esac`** (`case` spelled backwards!).
* **Pattern Alternation (`|`):** Multiple patterns sharing the same branch are separated by a **vertical bar (`|`)**, followed by a closing parenthesis **`)`**.
* **Branch Terminator (`;;`):** Every pattern branch (except optionally the last) must end with a **double semicolon (`;;`)**.
* **Default Catch-All (`*)`):** The asterisk **`*)`** matches **all values that do not match the known patterns** (equivalent to `default:` in C/Java).
key_takeaways: In a Bash 'if command; then ... fi' statement, the 'then' block executes ONLY when the command following 'if' returns an exit status code of 0!
A multi-branch 'case' statement starts with 'case $var in' and ends with 'esac'.
In 'case', multiple patterns are separated by '|', each branch ends with ';;', and '*)' serves as the default catch-all branch.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: In C/Python, 0 is False and 1 is True; in Bash 'if command', exit status code 0 means SUCCESS (True, executes 'then'), while any non-zero exit code (1–255) means FAILURE (False)!
EXAM TRAP: Do not forget ';;' at the end of each pattern block and 'esac' at the end of a 'case' statement.

lecture.title: Loop Statements (`for`, `while`, `until`), `break`/`continue`, Debugging (`bash -x`) & Best Practices
objectives: Write `for` (shell-style & C-style), `while`, and `until` loops, including the official Odd Accumulator (`{1..100..2}`) and 9×9 Multiplication Table scripts
Control loop execution with `break` (exit entire loop) and `continue` (skip current round to next iteration)
Debug shell scripts using `#!/bin/bash -x` / `bash -x`, evaluate `$?` exit status codes (`0` vs. `2` for missing file in `ls`), and apply shell coding style best practices
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Loop Statements: `for`, `while`, and `until` Bash provides three loop constructs (**`for`**, **`while`**, **`until`**), all using **`do ... done`** for the loop body, plus **`break`** and **`continue`**: | Loop / Control | Syntax & Official Examples (Ch.06, pp. 359–367) | | :--- | :--- | | **`for` (Shell style)** | `for var in list; do commands; done`
• List forms: `host1 host2 host3`, brace range **`host{1..3}`**, step range **`{1..100..2}`**, command substitution **`$(seq 2 2 8)`** or **`$(ls)`**. | | **`for` (C style)** | `for (( i = 1; i <= 9; i++ )); do ... done` (used in the 9×9 Multiplication Table script). | | **`while` Loop** | Pre-test loop that repeats **while the condition is TRUE**:
`sum=0; i=1; while (( i <= 100 )); do let "sum+=i"; let "i += 2"; done` | | **`until` Loop** | Repeats **until the exit condition becomes TRUE** (runs while condition is FALSE):
`sum=0; i=1; until (( i > 100 )); do let "sum+=i"; let "i += 2"; done` | | **`break` vs. `continue`** | • **`break`**: Immediately **interrupts and exits the entire loop** (e.g., find first number divisible by 5: `if (( i % 5 == 0 )); then break; fi`).
• **`continue`**: **Skips the rest of the current iteration** and starts the next round of the loop (e.g., skip numbers divisible by 3: `if (( i % 3 == 0 )); then continue; fi`). | * **Official Odd Accumulator Script (`1 + 3 + 5 + ... + 99 = 2500` — Ch.06, p.361):** ```bash #!/bin/bash sum=0 for i in {1..100..2} do let "sum+=i" done echo "sum=$sum" ``` --- ### 2. Debugging Mode (`-x`) & Exit Status Codes (`$?`) * **Activating Bash Debugging Mode (2 Ways — Ch.06, pp. 370–371):** 1. Add **`-x`** to the shebang line inside the script: **`#!/bin/bash -x`** 2. Invoke `bash` with **`-x`** from the CLI: **`bash -x adder.sh`** * *Effect:* Prints each command and expanded variable values in real time (prefixed with `+`) before executing it! * **Evaluating Exit Status Codes (`$?` — Ch.06, pp. 372–373):** * Every command returns an exit code stored in **`$?`**. * **`0`** indicates success (`ls /etc/hosts` -> `echo $?` outputs **`0`**). * Non-zero indicates an error (`ls /etc/nofile` -> `echo $?` outputs **`2`**). * Use **`exit `** (e.g., `exit 1`) inside a script to terminate immediately and return exit code `` to the caller. --- ### 3. Shell Coding Style Best Practices (Ch.06, pp. 374–376) * Break long one-liners into readable multi-line steps using descriptive intermediate variables (`PACKAGETYPE=kernel`, `INSTALLEPOCH=...`, `INSTALLDATETIME=...`). * Align `if/fi` and `do/done`, indent nested blocks, add comments (`#`), and use blank lines to separate logical sections.
key_takeaways: while (( i <= 100 )) loops while the condition is true; until (( i > 100 )) loops until the condition becomes true.
break exits the entire loop immediately, whereas continue skips only the current iteration and proceeds to the next loop round.
Enable script trace debugging with '#!/bin/bash -x' or 'bash -x script.sh'; check the previous command's exit status code with 'echo $?' (0 = success).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse 'while' and 'until' conditions! For the Odd Accumulator (1 to 100), 'while' uses 'while (( i <= 100 ))', whereas 'until' uses the opposite termination condition 'until (( i > 100 ))'!
EXAM TRAP: When 'ls' fails because a file does not exist ('ls /etc/nofile'), 'echo $?' outputs 2 (Ch.06 p.372).

objectives: Distinguish the two core Linux kernel container features: Namespaces (resource isolation across 6 types) and `cgroups` (resource limitation in `/sys/fs/cgroup`)
Explain what `iSula` (`iSulad`) is, why it is written in C/C++ instead of Go, and its Northbound (CLI/CRI) and Southbound (OCI: LCR, runC, Kata) architecture
Quantify iSula's Lightweight (68%+ less memory), Fast (35% faster startup, 75% faster download, 15% faster `isula-build`), Easy-to-Use (`isula-transform`), and Flexible (REST vs. gRPC) advantages
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Core Linux Kernel Container Primitives: Namespaces vs. `cgroups`
Container technology evolved from `chroot` (1982), FreeBSD `Jail` (1998), `Linux-VServer` (2001), `Solaris Zone` (2004), `OpenVZ` (2005), **`cgroups` & `Namespaces` (2007)**, `LXC` (2008), to `Docker`, **`iSula`**, and `Kubernetes` (2011–now).
* **Namespaces — Function: Resource Isolation (Ch.07, p.391):**
  Encapsulates global kernel resources so processes in different namespaces are isolated from each other:

| Namespace Type | System Call Parameter | Isolated Resource | Kernel Version |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PID namespace** | `CLONE_NEWPID` | Process IDs | Linux 2.6.24 |
| **Mount namespace** | `CLONE_NEWNS` | File system mount points | Linux 2.6.19 |
| **Network namespace** | `CLONE_NEWNET` | Network devices, IP addresses, ports | Linux 2.6.24–2.6.29 |
| **User namespace** | `CLONE_NEWUSER` | User IDs (UIDs) and Group IDs (GIDs) | Linux 2.6.23–3.8 |
| **UTS namespace** | `CLONE_NEWUTS` | **Host names and domain names** | Linux 2.6.19 |
| **IPC namespace** | `CLONE_NEWIPC` | Semaphores, message queues, shared memory | Linux 2.6.19 |

* **`cgroups` (Linux Control Groups) — Function: Resource Limitation (Ch.07, p.392):**
  * **Limits system resources** (CPU, memory, block I/O) available to a set of processes, controls process priorities, and suspends/restores processes.
  * Organized as files and directories in **`/sys/fs/cgroup`**.

---

### 2. What is `iSula` / `iSulad` & Its Unified Architecture
* **Why `iSula`?** Mainstream engines like Docker and containerd are written in **Go**, which incurs high memory overhead in resource-constrained edge computing, IoT, and high-density server scenarios. **`iSula`** is openEuler's native container solution implemented in **C/C++**, featuring a unified architecture for CT and IT fields (system, secure, common, and embedded containers).
* **iSulad Architecture (Ch.07, p.394):**
  * **Northbound Interfaces:** **CLI (`isula`)** and **CRI** (for Kubernetes orchestration).
  * **Communication Modes:** **Lightweight mode (REST interface)** and **Performance mode (gRPC interface)**.
  * **Core Daemon (`iSulad`):** Image Service, Execution Service, Content Service, and Rootfs Service (separated to isolate operations).
  * **Southbound OCI Runtimes:** Interconnects with OCI-compliant runtimes: **LCR (Lightweight Container Runtime — default, written in C)**, **`runC`**, and **`Kata`**.

---

### 3. Four Advantages of iSula (Lightweight, Fast, Easy-to-Use, Flexible)
1. **Lightweight:** **>68% lower stable memory usage** for 100 containers compared to Docker (C/C++, LCR, simplified monitor process).
2. **Fast:**
   * **35% faster concurrent startup** (100 containers) using `fork/exec` + direct function calls and separated rootfs/image services.
   * **75% faster image download** via smart on-demand loading.
   * **15% faster image building (`isula-build`)** via **DAG-based building** (unlike `docker build`, `isula-build` does **not** start a container for every Dockerfile instruction—only for necessary instructions like `RUN`).
3. **Easy-to-Use Toolkit:** **`isula-build`** (Dockerfile image builder) and **`isula-transform`** (cold/live migration tool converting Docker containers to iSulad).
key_takeaways: Namespaces provide resource ISOLATION (6 types: PID, Mount, Network, User, UTS [host/domain names], IPC), whereas cgroups (/sys/fs/cgroup) provide resource LIMITATION (CPU, memory, block I/O).
iSula (iSulad) is written in C/C++ (unlike Go-based Docker), uses LCR as its default OCI runtime, and supports Lightweight mode (REST) and Performance mode (gRPC).

Compared with Docker, iSula reduces 100-container memory usage by >68%, speeds up concurrent startup by 35%, accelerates smart image downloads by 75%, and speeds up DAG-based image builds (isula-build) by 15%.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse Namespaces vs. cgroups! Namespaces = Resource Isolation (what a container can SEE); cgroups = Resource Limitation (how much CPU/RAM/I/O a container can USE).
EXAM TRAP: UTS namespace (CLONE_NEWUTS) isolates host names and domain names, whereas IPC namespace (CLONE_NEWIPC) isolates semaphores, message queues, and shared memory.

lecture.title: iSula Installation, Configuration Priority & Container Lifecycle Operations
objectives: Install `iSulad` via `yum`/`rpm` and apply the configuration priority order (`CLI > /etc/isulad/daemon.json > default code configurations`)
Identify the 4 official container states (`Created`, `Up`, `Paused`, `Exited` — Official Ch.07 Quiz Q1!)

Execute `isula` container lifecycle commands: `create`, `start`, `run` (`-d`, `-it`, `-p`, `-e`, `--workdir`, `--name`, `--dns`, `--restart`, `--rm`), `pause`/`unpause`, `exec`, `ps`, `inspect`, `logs`, `restart`, and `rm`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Installing & Configuring `iSulad` (Configuration Priority Rule!) * **Installation:** * Recommended (auto-resolves dependencies): **`yum install -y iSulad`** (installs iSula 2.0.11 by default on openEuler 22.03 LTS). * Offline RPM (must manually install all dependency RPMs): `rpm -ihv iSulad-xx.aarch64.rpm`. * **Configuration Priority (Highest to Lowest — Ch.07, p.401):** $CLI (`isulad --xxx)` > Configuration file (`/etc/isulad/daemon.json)` > Default configurations in code$ * **CLI Configuration:** e.g., **`isulad -l DEBUG`** (takes effect immediately without restarting; if managed by `systemd`, modifying `OPTIONS` in **`/etc/sysconfig/iSulad`** is equivalent to CLI configuration). * **Config File (`/etc/isulad/daemon.json`):** Modifying `/etc/isulad/daemon.json` **requires restarting `iSulad`** (**`systemctl restart isulad`**) to take effect! --- ### 2. Container Lifecycle & 4 Official Container States (Ch.07 Quiz Q1!) * **Official Ch.07 Quiz Q1 (p.439):** Which of the following are container states? * **`A. Created`** (newly created via `isula create nginx`, not yet started) * **`B. Exited`** (stopped container) * **`C. Up`** (running container after `isula start` or `isula run`) * **`D. Paused`** (suspended via `isula pause`) -> **Answer: `ABCD`!** --- ### 3. Complete `isula` Container Lifecycle Commands | Command | Key Options & Usage Examples (Ch.07, pp. 405–417) | | :--- | :--- | | **`isula create `** | Creates a container in `Created` state; returns a 64-hex-digit Container ID (first **12 digits** shown in `isula ps`; can use unambiguous prefix like `e` or `7a`). | | **`isula start `** | Starts a `Created` or `Exited` container -> status changes to **`Up`**. | | **`isula run [opts] `** | Creates and starts a container in one step:
• **`-d`**: Run in background.
• **`-it`**: Interactive (`-i`) + allocate pseudo-TTY (`-t`), e.g., `isula run -it nginx /bin/bash`.
• **`-p hostPort:containerPort[/udp]`**: Port mapping (can pass multiple `-p`, e.g., `isula run -d -p 8081:80 -p 5000:5000 nginx`).
• **`-e KEY=VAL`**: Set environment variable(s) (`-e A=100 -e B=200`).
• **`--workdir /tmp`**: Set container working directory.
• **`--name test`**: Assign container name.
• **`--dns 114.114.114.114`**: Set container DNS server.
• **`--restart `**: Auto-restart policy: **`no`** (default), **`on-failure[:N]`**, **`always`**, **`unless-stopped`**.
• **`--rm`**: Automatically delete container when it stops. | | **`isula pause / unpause`** | `isula pause ` pauses a running container (`Paused`); `isula unpause ` resumes it (`Up`). | | **`isula exec` vs. `attach`** | **`isula exec [-it] `** creates a new terminal to run commands cleanly (**recommended**; `attach` may cause errors and is not recommended). | | **`isula ps`** | Lists running containers. **`-a`** (all containers), **`-q`** (only IDs), **`-n 2`** (latest 2 created containers). | | **`isula inspect / logs`** | **`isula inspect [--format="{{json .NetworkSettings}}"] `** (Go template format by default); **`isula logs `**. | | **`isula restart / rm`** | **`isula restart `**; **`isula rm `** deletes stopped containers (**`isula rm -f `** forcibly deletes a running container!). |
key_takeaways: iSulad configuration priority from highest to lowest is: CLI (isulad --xxx or /etc/sysconfig/iSulad OPTIONS) > Configuration file (/etc/isulad/daemon.json) > Default code configurations.
All four states—Created, Exited, Up, and Paused—are valid iSula container states (Official Ch.07 Quiz Q1: ABCD).
isula rm can only delete stopped containers by default; use 'isula rm -f <ID>' to forcibly delete a running container, or '--rm' on 'isula run' to auto-delete upon exit.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Official Ch.07 Quiz Q1): 'Which of the following are container states? A. Created B. Exited C. Up D. Paused' -> ABCD!
EXAM TRAP: In 'isula run -p 8081:80 nginx', the FIRST number (8081) is the HOST port and the SECOND number (80) is the CONTAINER port!

lecture.title: iSula Container Networking (CNI) & Persistent Storage (`-v`)
objectives: Explain how `iSulad` integrates with Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins and configure CNI in `/etc/isulad/daemon.json`
Distinguish the 3 iSula CNI plugins (`bridge`, `portmap`, `firewall`) and manage networks via `isula network create/ls/inspect` and `--net`
Implement container persistent storage by mounting host files/directories with `isula run -v /host:/container[:rw|:ro]`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. How `iSulad` Implements Container Networking with CNI
* **Runtime & Network Flow:** `User -> iSula -> Runtime (LCR by default) / CNI / CSI -> Container`.
* Because `iSulad` does not bundle a built-in network stack, it uses **CNI (Container Network Interface)** binary plugins (v0.9.0+ recommended, v1.3.0 available from `github.com/containernetworking/plugins`).
* **Supported Network Mode:** While CNI specifications support bridge, VLAN, Flannel, and Calico, **currently `iSula` only supports the `bridge` mode** (Ch.07, p.420), where containers connected to the same Linux bridge communicate directly with each other and with the host.
* **Enabling CNI in `/etc/isulad/daemon.json` (Ch.07, p.422):**
  * **`"network-plugin": "cni"`** (can be set to `cni` or left empty by default).
  * **`"cni-bin-dir": "/opt/cni/bin"`** (default directory storing compiled CNI plugin binaries).
  * **`"cni-conf-dir": "/etc/cni/net.d"`** (default directory storing CNI network configuration files).

---

### 2. Three iSula Network Plugins & `isula network` Commands
When you create a bridge network in iSula, three CNI plugins work together (Ch.07, p.423):
1. **`bridge` plugin:** Creates a Linux bridge device, connects container virtual NICs to the bridge, and assigns IP addresses via the **`host-local` IPAM** plugin.
2. **`portmap` plugin:** Implements **NAT port forwarding** between container ports and host ports.
3. **`firewall` plugin:** Uses **`iptables`** to control ingress/egress container traffic and enforce port-mapping security rules.
* **iSula Network CLI Operations:**
  ```bash
  isula network create cni0
  isula network ls
  isula network inspect cni0
  isula run --net cni0 -d -it isulad/busybox sleep 99d
  ```

---

### 3. Container Persistent Storage (`-v` Host Bind Mounts & SCI)
By default, modifications inside a container are written only to its **temporary read/write container layer** and are lost when the container is deleted!
* **Two Persistent Storage Methods:**
  1. **Mount host files or directories into the container (`-v`).**
  2. **Use a third-party storage plugin** (invoked via **SCI**).
* **Mounting Syntax & Permissions (`-v` on `isula create` or `isula run`):**
  ```bash
  isula run -it -n storage \
    -v /root/test1.txt:/tmp/test1.txt:rw \
    -v /root/test2.txt:/tmp/test2.txt:ro \
    oepkgs/test/nginx:latest /bin/bash
  ```
  * **`rw` (Default):** Container has **read-write** permission on the mounted host file/directory.
  * **`ro`:** Container has **read-only** permission (writing inside the container returns `Read-only file system`).
key_takeaways: iSulad uses LCR as its default runtime and CNI for networking; currently, iSula only supports the 'bridge' network mode.

In /etc/isulad/daemon.json, CNI is configured with 'network-plugin': 'cni', 'cni-bin-dir': '/opt/cni/bin' (default), and 'cni-conf-dir': '/etc/cni/net.d' (default), utilizing the bridge, portmap, and firewall plugins.
Use 'isula run -v /host/path:/container/path[:rw|:ro]' for persistent storage; 'rw' (read-write) is the default mount permission.

EXAM TRAP: Currently, iSula only supports the 'bridge' network mode in CNI (Ch.07 p.420).

lecture.title: Container Image Architecture (UnionFS, AUFS, OverlayFS) & Image Management (`isula images/pull/tag/rmi`)
objectives: Explain the layered container image structure (read-only `rootfs` image layers up to 128 layers + read/write container layer) and Copy-on-Write (CoW)
Compare UnionFS implementations: AUFS (`aufs/diff` & `aufs/mnt`) vs. OverlayFS (`lowerdir`, `upperdir`, `merged`, `workdir`, `copy_up`, and whiteout/opaque files)
Parse image naming (`[registry/][path/]<imagename>[:tag]`) and manage images with `isula images`, `isula inspect`, `isula pull`, `isula tag`, and `isula rmi`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Container Image Architecture, Layer Limit & Copy-on-Write (CoW)
* **What is in a Container Image?** A container image is an immutable template containing a complete operating system **`rootfs` (files and directories)** plus the application and its dependencies.
  * **Shared Host Kernel:** All containers share the **host OS kernel** and **cannot modify the host kernel**.
  * **Layer Limit:** An image is immutable and **cannot exceed 128 layers** (Ch.07, p.428).
* **Image Layers vs. Container Layer & Copy-on-Write (CoW — Ch.07, pp. 429–430):**
  * **Image layers (Read-Only / R/O):** Shared across containers; enables incremental pulls/storage.
  * **Container layer (Thin Read/Write / R/W layer):** Mounted on top when a container starts.
  * **4 File Operations under CoW:**
    1. **Creating a file:** Added directly to the top R/W **container layer**.
    2. **Reading a file:** Searched from top layer (`upperdir`/container layer) down to lower image layers (`lowerdir`).
    3. **Modifying a file:** Looked up from top to bottom; when modified for the first time, the file is **copied from the read-only image layer up to the container layer (`copy_up`)** and modified there (**Copy-on-Write**).
    4. **Deleting a file/directory:** Because image layers are read-only, UnionFS creates a **whiteout file** (or **opaque directory** in OverlayFS) in the R/W container layer to hide the underlying file/directory!

---

### 2. UnionFS Drivers: AUFS vs. OverlayFS
**UnionFS** mounts multiple directories (branches/layers) onto a single unified virtual mount point:
* **AUFS (Advanced Multi-Layered Unification Filesystem — Ch.07, p.432):**
  * Stores each image layer and container layer in `/var/lib/xxx/aufs/diff/<ID>`, and presents the unified working directory at **`/var/lib/xxx/aufs/mnt`**.
* **OverlayFS (`overlay` / `overlay2` — Ch.07, p.433):**
  * Simpler deployment and higher performance than AUFS; built on top of `ext4` or `xfs` using **four directories**:
    1. **`lowerdir`:** Read-only image layers (`lowerdir1`, `lowerdir2`...).
    2. **`upperdir`:** Read-write container layer (stores new, `copy_up`-modified, and whiteout/opaque files).
    3. **`merged`:** Unified view presented to the user/container.
    4. **`workdir`:** Internal working directory (**invisible to users**).

---

### 3. Container Image Naming & `isula` Image Commands
* **Image Naming Format:** **`[registry/][path/]<imagename>[:tag]`**
  * If `registry/` is omitted, the configured default public/mirror registry is used.
  * If `:tag` is omitted, **`latest`** is used by default!
* **`isula` Image Management Commands (Ch.07, pp. 435–438):**
  * **`isula images`:** Lists local images on the host.
  * **`isula inspect <image:tag>`:** Views detailed JSON metadata (e.g., `isula inspect nginx:latest`).
  * **`isula pull <image>`:** Pulls an image from a registry (`isula pull openeuler/busybox:latest`).
    * **CRITICAL EXAM TRAP (Ch.07, p.436):** **`iSula` supports the `pull` command and does NOT support the `push` command!**
  * **`isula tag <source_image:tag> <target_image:tag>`:** Creates a new tag alias referring to the same `IMAGE ID` (e.g., `isula tag openeuler/busybox:latest busybox:test`).
  * **`isula rmi <image:tag>`:** Deletes an image from the host (`isula rmi busybox:test`).
key_takeaways: Container images encapsulate the OS rootfs and app dependencies while sharing the host OS kernel; an image is read-only/immutable and cannot exceed 128 layers.

OverlayFS uses four directories: lowerdir (R/O image layers), upperdir (R/W container layer), merged (unified container view), and workdir (invisible to users), using copy_up (CoW) for modifications and whiteout files / opaque directories for deletions.

In '[registry/][path/]<imagename>[:tag]', the default tag is 'latest'; manage images with 'isula images', 'isula pull', 'isula tag', 'isula inspect', and 'isula rmi' (Note: iSula does NOT support 'push'!).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.07 p.436): iSula supports 'isula pull', but DOES NOT support 'isula push'!

EXAM TRAP: Deleting a file inside a container does NOT delete it from the read-only image layer (lowerdir)—instead, AUFS/OverlayFS creates a 'whiteout' file (or 'opaque' directory) in the container layer (upperdir) to mask it.
