quiz_questions.question: What is the maximum number of layers a container image can have, and what Happens when a file inside a read-only image layer (`lowerdir`) is deleted inside a running container?
options: A. Max 32 layers; the file is physically erased from `lowerdir` on the host disk
B. Max 128 layers; UnionFS (AUFS/OverlayFS) creates a `whiteout` file in the R/W container layer (`upperdir`) to hide the deleted file
C. Max 1024 layers; the host kernel is recompiled
D. Max 4 layers; the container immediately crashes
quiz_questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p.428 & p.430–433), an image is immutable and cannot exceed 128 layers. When a file is deleted in a container, UnionFS creates a whiteout file at the R/W container layer (`upperdir`) to block/hide the file without altering the read-only image layer.

quiz_questions.question: Which four directories are used by `OverlayFS` to construct a union file system, and which one is invisible to users?
quiz_questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p.433), OverlayFS is constructed and implemented using the `lowerdir`, `upperdir`, `merged`, and `workdir` directories, where `workdir` is invisible to users.

quiz_questions.question: Which of the following statements about container image naming and `isula` image commands are TRUE?
options: A. In `[registry/][path/]<imagename>[:tag]`, if `:tag` is not specified, `latest` is used by default.
B. `isula` supports the `isula pull` command to download images, and does NOT support the `push` command.
C. `isula tag openeuler/busybox:latest busybox:test` modifies/adds image tag information.
D. `isula rmi <image>` deletes an image on the host.
quiz_questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp.434–438), all four statements are explicitly documented in the official Huawei training material.

mock_exam.title: HCIA-openEuler V2.0 — National Stage Final Mock Exam
mock_exam.instructions: 60 Questions in 60 Minutes: 20 Single-Choice (15 pts each), 20 Multiple-Choice (20 pts each, strict all-or-nothing grading), 10 True/False (10 pts each), and 10 Hands-On openEuler/Shell/iSula Labs (20 pts each).

questions.question: (Official Ch.02 Quiz Q2) Which of the following keys can be used in the openEuler Bash shell to quickly supplement (auto-complete) commands, options, and file parameters?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.02 (p. 50 & p. 52), pressing Tab automatically completes commands, parameters, or filenames (pressing Tab twice lists all matching commands).

questions.question: In the openEuler source code repository, which directory explicitly declares all open-source licenses in use, and what is China's first open-source license adopted by openEuler?
options: B. LICENSES directory; Mulan PSL (Mulan Permissive Software License)
questions.explanation: Per Ch.02 (p. 29 & p. 35), in the openEuler code repository the `LICENSES` directory declares the open-source licenses in use, and Mulan is China's first open-source license adopted by openEuler.

questions.question: (Official Ch.03 Quiz Q1) How many lines of a file are displayed by default when running the `head` command without any `-n` option?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (p. 98, p. 141 & p. 151), both `head` and `tail` display 10 lines by default when no line count is specified.

questions.question: Which Linux virtual directory is a direct mapping of system kernel and memory state, allowing administrators to read CPU, memory, and process info directly?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (p. 80), `/proc` is a virtual directory mapping system memory; `/etc` holds configuration files, `/var` stores variable logs/spool data, and `/opt` stores third-party optional applications.

questions.question: When creating links with `ln`, what happens if you create a symbolic (soft) link with `ln -s target linkname` and later delete the original `target` file?
options: A. The soft link remains valid and retains a full copy of the original file data
B. The soft link becomes a dangling/invalid link because it only stores the path to the target
C. The kernel automatically converts the soft link into a hard link
D. Both the target and link share the same inode, so data cannot be removed until linkname is deleted
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 115–116), a soft link points to a file path (different inode) and becomes invalid if the source file is deleted, whereas a hard link (`ln` without `-s`) shares the same inode and keeps the data intact until all hard links are deleted.

questions.question: In Vim Command-line (Last-line) mode, which command globally replaces all occurrences of `foo` with `bar` across the entire file?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (p. 129), `%` targets all lines in the file and the `g` flag replaces all matches on each line (`:%s/foo/bar/g`).

questions.question: (Official Ch.04 Quiz Q1) Which of the following commands can be used to dynamically check host resource usage (CPU, memory, load average, and running processes) in real time?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (p. 249), `top` dynamically monitors real-time CPU, memory, and process resource usage; `ps` shows a static snapshot, `free` displays memory only, and `lscpu` displays CPU hardware architecture.

questions.question: If the current shell `umask` is `0022`, what are the default numeric permissions assigned to a newly created regular file and a newly created directory respectively?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (p. 183), default base permissions are `666` for regular files (no execute bit by default) and `777` for directories. Subtracting `022` gives `644` (`rw-r--r--`) for files and `755` (`rwxr-xr-x`) for directories.

questions.question: In `/etc/passwd`, which two colon-separated columns represent the user's UID and login shell respectively?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (p. 161), `/etc/passwd` has 7 fields: `1:username`, `2:password placeholder (x)`, `3:UID`, `4:GID`, `5:description`, `6:home directory`, `7:login shell`.

questions.question: When sending process termination signals using `kill`, what is the key difference between signal `15 (SIGTERM)` and signal `9 (SIGKILL)`?
options: A. Signal 15 pauses a process; Signal 9 resumes it
B. Signal 15 requests graceful termination (can be caught/ignored); Signal 9 forces unconditional immediate termination by the kernel
C. Signal 9 reloads configuration files without stopping the PID
D. Signal 15 can only be executed by root, while Signal 9 is for regular users
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (p. 234), Signal 15 (`SIGTERM`, default for `kill PID`) allows a process to clean up and exit gracefully, whereas Signal 9 (`SIGKILL`) cannot be caught or ignored and terminates the process unconditionally.

questions.question: (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q2) Which of the following commands correctly formats the `/dev/hdb6` partition with the ext4 file system?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (p. 279 & p. 318), `mkfs -t <fstype> <device>` (or `mkfs.ext4 /dev/hdb6`) formats a partition on openEuler.

questions.question: Under the traditional MBR disk partitioning scheme for a SCSI disk, what are the maximum disk capacity and partition limits?
options: A. Max 16 TB; up to 128 primary partitions
B. Max 2 TB; up to 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended) and at most 15 partitions total on a SCSI disk
C. Max 2 TB; unlimited primary partitions
D. Max 4 TB; up to 8 primary partitions
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 269 & 273), MBR has a 2 TB limit and allows up to 4 primary partitions (or 3 primary + 1 extended containing logical partitions, capped at 15 total partitions on SCSI disks), whereas GPT breaks the 2 TB limit and supports 128 primary partitions.

questions.question: In LVM online expansion of an `xfs` file system after running `lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg01/lv01`, which command grows the XFS file system to occupy the newly added space?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (p. 298), `resize2fs` resizes ext2/ext3/ext4 file systems, while `xfs_growfs <mount_point>` (or `xfs_growfs <lv_device>`) expands mounted XFS file systems online.

questions.question: When shrinking an ext4 Logical Volume (LV) offline, what is the mandatory safe sequence of operations?
options: B. umount -> e2fsck -f -> resize2fs -> lvreduce -> mount
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (p. 299), you MUST unmount first (`umount`), check the filesystem (`e2fsck -f`), shrink the filesystem (`resize2fs`), shrink the LV (`lvreduce`), and finally remount (`mount`). Shrinking the LV before shrinking the filesystem destroys data!

questions.question: (Official Ch.06 Quiz Q1) What is the meaning of the `*` operator in a shell script arithmetic expression such as `$((a * b))`?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (p. 351 & p. 379), `*` performs arithmetic multiplication in shell arithmetic expressions (note: when using `expr`, `*` must be escaped as `\*` to avoid shell glob expansion).

questions.question: Which special Bash variable retrieves the exit code of the most recently executed foreground command, and which value indicates success?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (p. 372), `$?` stores the exit status of the previous command, where `0` means success and any non-zero value (1–255) indicates an error.

questions.question: Which Bash command-line flag executes a shell script in debugging mode, printing each expanded command prefixed with `+` before executing it?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 370–371), `bash -x script.sh` enables execution tracing (debugging mode), printing each command and its expanded arguments prior to execution.

questions.question: What is the configuration precedence order (highest to lowest priority) for the `iSulad` container daemon?
options: A. /etc/isulad/daemon.json > CLI arguments > default code settings
B. CLI arguments (or /etc/sysconfig/iSulad OPTIONS) > /etc/isulad/daemon.json > default configurations in code
C. Default configurations in code > /etc/isulad/daemon.json > CLI arguments
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p. 401), iSulad configuration priority is strictly: `CLI > configuration file (/etc/isulad/daemon.json) > default configurations in code`. Modifying `OPTIONS` in `/etc/sysconfig/iSulad` is equivalent to CLI configuration.

questions.question: In the `OverlayFS` union file system used by container images, which directory acts as an internal scratch directory and is invisible to users?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p. 433), OverlayFS uses `lowerdir` (read-only image layers), `upperdir` (writable container layer), `merged` (unified mount point), and `workdir` (internal helper directory invisible to users).

questions.question: Which southbound OCI container runtime does `iSulad` use by default, and which network mode does `iSula` currently support with CNI?
options: B. LCR (Lightweight Container Runtime); bridge network mode
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p. 394 & p. 420), iSula uses LCR as its default southbound OCI runtime (while also supporting runC/Kata) and currently supports `bridge` mode for CNI networking.

questions.chapter: Ch.01 OS for the AI Era
questions.question: Which of the following are core intelligent O&M and AI capabilities provided by the `openEuler Intelligence` platform?
options: A. Intelligent Q&A (Natural language interaction, OCR, and knowledge retrieval via RAG)
B. AI Application Development Framework (Agents and workflow orchestration)
C. Intelligent Optimization (AI-assisted parameter tuning and performance optimization)
D. Intelligent Diagnosis & Intelligent Container Image analysis
questions.explanation: Per Ch.01 (pp. 8–16), openEuler Intelligence delivers all four capability pillars: Intelligent Q&A, AI Application Development Framework, Intelligent Optimization, Intelligent Diagnosis, and Intelligent Container Images.

questions.question: According to Richard Stallman and the Free Software Foundation (FSF), which four essential freedoms define Free Software?
options: A. Freedom to run the program for any purpose
B. Freedom to study/learn how the program works and modify the source code
C. Freedom to redistribute copies of the program
D. Freedom to create and distribute modified derivative versions
questions.explanation: Per Ch.02 (p. 29), FSF defines four freedoms: run for any purpose (0), learn and modify source code (1), redistribute programs (2), and create/distribute derivatives (3).

questions.question: Which of the following statements about openEuler releases and licenses are TRUE?
options: A. Mulan PSL covers five major aspects: copyright license, patent license, non-trademark license, distribution restriction, and disclaimer/liability limitation.
B. BSD permits modifying, redistributing, and developing commercial software based on the open-source code.
C. Before contributing code to the openEuler community on Gitee, contributors must sign a Contributor License Agreement (CLA).
D. openEuler Innovation releases receive a 6-year enterprise support lifecycle, whereas LTS releases receive only 6 months.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.02 (pp. 29–36), A, B, and C are true. D is reversed: openEuler LTS (Long Term Support) versions are released every 2 years with long-term maintenance, while Innovation versions are released every 6 months with shorter maintenance.

questions.question: Which of the following help commands can be used on openEuler to inspect command usage, manuals, or brief one-line descriptions?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 65–69), `man` queries `/usr/share/man/*.gz` manual pages, `--help` queries external command options, `help` queries shell built-in commands, and `whatis` prints a brief summary from the man database.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about `tar` and `gzip` archive/compression operations on openEuler are TRUE?
options: A. `gzip` typically achieves a 60%–70% compression ratio and replaces the original uncompressed file with a `.gz` file by default.
B. `tar -czvf backup.tar.gz /etc/hosts` creates a gzip-compressed tar archive.
C. `tar -tf backup.tar.gz` lists the contents of an archive without extracting it.
D. `tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp` extracts the archive into `/tmp`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 111–114), all four statements accurately describe `gzip` and `tar` flags (`-c` create, `-x` extract, `-t` list, `-z` gzip, `-v` verbose, `-f` archive file, `-C` target directory).

questions.question: Which of the following Linux text processing commands and options are matched with their TRUE functions?
options: A. `grep -i` performs case-insensitive pattern matching; `grep -v` inverts the match (prints non-matching lines).
B. `cut -d ':' -f 1,7 /etc/passwd` extracts the 1st and 7th colon-delimited fields.
C. `wc -l` counts lines, while `sort -n -r` sorts numerically in descending order.
D. `awk -F ':' '{print $1}' /etc/passwd` prints the first field of each line using `:` as the field separator.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 143–147), all four statements accurately describe `grep`, `cut`, `wc`, `sort`, and `awk`.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Linux file types and `chmod`/`chown`/`sticky bit` permissions are TRUE?
options: A. The 7 Linux file types shown by `ls -l` are `-` (regular), `d` (directory), `l` (symlink), `b` (block), `c` (character), `p` (named pipe), and `s` (socket).
B. Setting the sticky bit (`chmod o+t /share` or `chmod 1777 /share`) ensures that only the file owner, directory owner, or root can delete or rename files inside `/share`.
C. `chown -R user1:group1 /data` recursively changes both the owner and the owning group of `/data`.
D. If `ls -l` displays a `+` sign right after the permission string (e.g., `-rw-r--r--+`), the file has an extended Access Control List (ACL) configured.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 172, 178–185), all four statements are directly confirmed in the official openEuler System Configuration chapter.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about RPM and DNF software package management on openEuler are TRUE?
options: A. `rpm -qa` queries all installed RPM packages, while `rpm -qf /usr/bin/vim` queries which package owns that file.
B. `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf` is the main global configuration file for DNF, and repository `.repo` files reside in `/etc/yum.repos.d/`.
C. Running `rpm -e --nodeps <pkg>` removes a package while ignoring dependencies, which may break dependent software.
D. `dnf` resolves package dependencies automatically, whereas `rpm -ivh` requires dependencies to be resolved manually.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 195–214), all four statements accurately contrast `rpm` and `dnf` operations on openEuler.

questions.question: Which of the following `systemctl` and `journald` commands are valid for managing services and inspecting logs on openEuler?
options: A. `systemctl enable --now httpd` enables the service at boot and starts it immediately.
B. `systemctl status sshd` displays the running status, PID, and recent log lines of `sshd`.
C. `journalctl -u sshd` queries systemd journal logs specifically for the `sshd` unit.
D. A standard systemd `.service` unit file contains three main sections: `[Unit]`, `[Service]`, and `[Install]`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 216–223), all four statements accurately describe `systemd`, `systemctl`, and `journald`.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about process scheduling priority (`nice`), background jobs, and scheduled tasks (`at`/`crontab`) are TRUE?
options: A. The `nice` value ranges from `-20` (highest priority) to `+19` (lowest priority), and only `root` can assign negative nice values.
B. Pressing `Ctrl+Z` suspends a foreground job and puts it in the background in Stopped state; `bg %1` resumes it in the background, and `fg %1` brings it back to the foreground.
C. `at` schedules a one-time task (`Ctrl+D` saves the job), while `crontab` schedules recurring periodic tasks using 5 time fields (`min hour dom month dow`).
D. Non-root users can execute `renice -n -10 -p <PID>` to increase the priority of any system process.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 229–248), A, B, and C are true. D is false because regular users can only lower priority (increase nice value toward +19) for their own processes; only `root` can assign negative nice values.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about persistent storage, `parted`, and `/etc/fstab` are TRUE?
options: A. On openEuler, `ext4` and `xfs` are common disk file systems; `blkid` and `lsblk -f` inspect block device UUIDs and file system types.
B. `parted` supports both MBR and GPT partitioning schemes and can run in both interactive mode and non-interactive script mode.
C. In `/etc/fstab`, the 6 columns in order are: Device/UUID, Mount Point, File System Type, Mount Options, Dump backup flag, and fsck Pass order.
D. Setting the `noatime` option in `/etc/fstab` disables updating access timestamps on reads and improves file system performance.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 257–282), all four statements match the official Storage Management slides.

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately describe Logical Volume Management (LVM) layers and commands on openEuler?
options: A. The LVM hierarchy flows bottom-up: Physical Disk/Partition -> Physical Volume (`pvcreate`) -> Volume Group (`vgcreate`) -> Logical Volume (`lvcreate`) -> File System (`mkfs`).
B. A Volume Group (VG) divides storage into fixed-size Physical Extents (PEs), which default to 4 MiB.
C. `vgextend vg01 /dev/sdc1` adds a new Physical Volume into an existing Volume Group `vg01`.
D. `lvcreate -L 10G -n lv_data vg01` creates a 10 GiB Logical Volume named `lv_data` inside `vg01`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 284–297), all four statements correctly describe LVM concepts and commands.

questions.question: Which of the following `nmcli` and network diagnostic commands are valid on openEuler?
options: A. `nmcli con add con-name "Euler" type Ethernet ifname enp3s0` creates a new Ethernet connection profile.
B. `nmcli con mod "Euler" +ipv4.routes "192.168.10.0/24 10.0.0.1"` appends a persistent static route to the connection.
C. `ss -tulnp` inspects listening TCP/UDP sockets along with their owning process PIDs.
D. `tracepath <destination>` traces the network hop path and path MTU to a remote host.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 308–317), all four statements accurately reflect NetworkManager (`nmcli`), `ss`, and `tracepath` usage on openEuler.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Bash I/O redirection, pipes, and quoting are TRUE?
options: A. File descriptors `0`, `1`, and `2` correspond to Standard Input (stdin), Standard Output (stdout), and Standard Error (stderr).
B. `command &> output.log` redirects both stdout and stderr to `output.log` (overwriting its content).
C. Single quotes (`'...'`) preserve literal characters and prevent variable/command expansion, whereas double quotes (`"..."`) allow `var` and `(cmd)` expansion.
D. A pipe (`cmd1 | cmd2`) sends the stdout of `cmd1` directly as the stdin of `cmd2`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 338–347), all four statements are true.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Bash variables, test conditions, and loops are TRUE?
options: A. `#` gives the number of positional arguments passed to a script, while `0` is the script's own name.
B. In `[ ... ]` test expressions, `-eq` and `-gt` compare integers, while `=` and `-z` evaluate strings.
C. `[ -d /etc/dnf ]` returns exit code 0 (true) if `/etc/dnf` exists and is a directory.
D. In loops, `break` exits the entire enclosing loop immediately, whereas `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 345–366), all four statements are core Bash scripting fundamentals covered in the training material.

questions.question: When comparing a `while` loop and an `until` loop in Bash, which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: A. A `while` loop continues executing as long as its test condition evaluates to TRUE (exit code 0).
B. An `until` loop continues executing as long as its test condition evaluates to FALSE (non-zero exit code), and stops once the condition becomes TRUE.
C. Both `while` and `until` loops enclose their loop body between `do` and `done`.
D. In `i++` (post-increment), the current value of `i` is returned first and then `i` is incremented by 1.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 353 & 365–367), all four statements are true.

questions.question: (Official Ch.07 Quiz Q1) Which of the following are valid container states in `iSula`?
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p. 439), all four (`Created`, `Exited`, `Up`, and `Paused`) are container states displayed by `isula ps -a`.

questions.question: Which Linux kernel mechanisms provide container isolation and resource limits, and what makes `iSula` distinct from Docker?
options: A. Linux `Namespaces` provide isolation (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS, User), while `cgroups` enforce CPU/memory/I/O resource quotas.
B. `iSulad` is written in C/C++ (unlike Go-based Docker), giving it a smaller memory footprint and ~35% faster concurrent container startup.
C. `iSula` provides northbound CLI and Kubernetes CRI interfaces and southbound OCI interfaces (`LCR`, `runC`, `Kata`).
D. `iSula` can manage both lightweight application containers and system containers.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp. 390–398), all four statements describe kernel container primitives and `iSula` architectural advantages.

questions.question: Which of the following `isula` CLI commands perform the stated container lifecycle operations?
options: A. `isula exec -it mybox /bin/sh` runs an interactive shell inside a running container named `mybox`.
B. `isula logs mybox` retrieves stdout/stderr logs generated by container `mybox`.
C. `isula inspect mybox` outputs detailed low-level JSON metadata (IP, mounts, state) for `mybox`.
D. `isula rm -f mybox` forcibly deletes a container (even if currently running).
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp. 405–417), all four `isula` lifecycle commands are valid and follow Docker-compatible CLI semantics.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about container image layering and Copy-on-Write (CoW) in `iSula` are TRUE?
options: A. A container image consists of read-only image layers (rootfs/app layers), and running a container mounts a thin read-write container layer on top.
B. When a container attempts to modify a file located in a read-only `lowerdir`, OverlayFS performs a `copy_up` operation to copy the file into `upperdir` before modifying it.
C. Deleting a file that resides in a read-only image layer creates a `whiteout` file in `upperdir` to hide it without modifying the underlying image.
D. `isula pull`, `isula tag`, `isula images`, and `isula rmi` manage local container images on the host.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp. 428–438), all four statements accurately describe UnionFS/OverlayFS CoW mechanics and image commands.

questions.chapter: Ch.01 OS for the AI Era
questions.question: (Official Ch.01 Quiz Q1) The `openEuler Intelligence` platform currently supports two interaction entries: Web entry and Intelligent Shell entry.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.01 (p. 8 & p. 20), openEuler Intelligence explicitly exposes two interaction entries: Web and Intelligent Shell.

questions.question: (Official Ch.02 Quiz Q1) You do not need to specify the password of the `root` user during the openEuler OS installation; however, you must specify the password of the `root` user when logging in to the OS after the installation.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.02 (p. 52), the official quiz states this is True (when root account is skipped or locked/deferred in installer if an admin user is created, or per the official quiz Q1 answer key: True).

questions.question: In the openEuler filesystem, `less` allows only forward (downward) page scrolling and cannot scroll backward, whereas `more` supports full bidirectional scrolling.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (p. 104 & pp. 137–139), it is the opposite: `more` only moves forward, while `less` supports both upward and downward scrolling as well as `/` and `?` searching.

questions.question: Running `locate myfile.conf` searches an internal file index database (`mlocate.db`), so newly created files may not appear until `updatedb` is executed.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 108–109), `locate` queries a pre-built database rather than scanning live disks like `find`, so `updatedb` must be run to index newly created files.

questions.question: The `su root` command switches identity to `root` AND resets all environment variables (including `PATH` and `HOME`) to `root`'s login environment, making it completely identical to `su - root`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (p. 191), `su` changes the user identity WITHOUT starting a login shell or loading the target user's environment variables, whereas `su -` (or `su -l`) switches to a full login shell with the target user's environment.

questions.question: Unlike `at`, which uses `cron` daemon configuration files, `crontab -e` edits a user's personal periodic schedule, and modifying it immediately notifies `crond` without requiring a service restart.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 244–247), editing crontab with `crontab -e` automatically updates and reloads the user's cron schedule in `crond`.

questions.question: (Official Ch.05 Quiz Q1) The `route` command can view or configure host route information, and route entries configured with `route add` remain valid permanently across system reboots.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (p. 318), routes added via the `route` command take effect temporarily in runtime kernel memory and are LOST upon reboot; use `nmcli` or route config files for persistence.

questions.question: (Official Ch.06 Quiz Q2) An administrator can run the `name==Tom` command in a Bash script to assign the value `Tom` to the variable `name`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (p. 346 & p. 379), variable assignment in Bash uses a single `=` with NO spaces around it (`name=Tom`), NOT `==`.

questions.question: If a shell script does not have execute (`+x`) permission, it cannot be invoked directly via `./script.sh`, but it can still be executed via `bash script.sh` or `sh script.sh`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (p. 334), `./script.sh` requires read+execute permission, whereas passing the file to an interpreter (`bash script.sh`) only requires read permission.

questions.question: A container started in `iSula` with `-v /root/test2.txt:/tmp/test2.txt:ro` allows processes inside the container to modify `/tmp/test2.txt` and persist those edits to the host.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (p. 426), the `:ro` mount option mounts the host path as **read-only** inside the container; `:rw` is required for read-write persistence.

questions.question: Lab 1 (Text Processing Pipeline): Complete the command pipeline to extract all lines from `/etc/passwd` whose login shell ends with `bash`, then print ONLY column 1 (username) and column 7 (shell) using `awk` with `:` as delimiter.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 144–145), `grep 'bash' /etc/passwd` matches lines ending with `bash`, and `awk -F ':' '{print 1, $7}'` splits on `:` to display username and shell.

questions.question: Lab 2 (Archive & Symbolic Link): Write two commands: (1) create a gzip-compressed tar archive `/tmp/etc_conf.tar.gz` from `/etc/hosts`, and (2) create a symbolic (soft) link `/tmp/hosts.link` pointing to `/etc/hosts`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.03 (pp. 113–117), `tar -czvf` creates a gzip-compressed archive and `ln -s` creates a symbolic link (omitting `-s` would create a hard link).

questions.question: Lab 3 (User & ACL Permissions): Write two commands: (1) add existing user `alice` to supplementary group `wheel` WITHOUT removing her existing groups, and (2) grant user `alice` read-write-execute (`rwx`) ACL permission on `/opt/app.log`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 168 & 187), `usermod -aG` appends a supplementary group (`-G` alone overwrites existing supplementary groups), and `setfacl -m u:alice:rwx` modifies the file ACL.

questions.question: Lab 4 (Systemd & Crontab): Write: (1) the command to enable and immediately start the `httpd` service, and (2) a `crontab` schedule line that runs `/usr/local/bin/backup.sh` every day at 02:30 AM.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.04 (pp. 220 & 245–246), `systemctl enable --now` enables boot startup and activates immediately; crontab fields are `minute(30) hour(2) dom(*) month(*) dow(*)`.

questions.question: Lab 5 (LVM Provisioning Workflow): Complete the 4-step LVM creation commands to initialize `/dev/sdb1` as a PV, create Volume Group `vg_data`, create a 20G Logical Volume `lv_app` inside `vg_data`, and format it as `ext4`.
questions.solution:
pvcreate /dev/sdb1
vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1
lvcreate -L 20G -n lv_app vg_data
mkfs -t ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_app
questions.answer: pvcreate /dev/sdb1; vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1; lvcreate -L 20G -n lv_app vg_data; mkfs -t ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_app
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 288–296), the LVM creation workflow is `pvcreate` -> `vgcreate` -> `lvcreate` -> `mkfs`.

questions.question: Lab 6 (Online LV Expansion & NetworkManager): Complete the commands to: (1) extend `/dev/vg_data/lv_app` by adding 10G and grow its `ext4` file system online, and (2) activate an `nmcli` connection named `Euler`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.05 (pp. 298 & 310), `lvextend -L +10G` expands the LV, `resize2fs` grows an `ext4` filesystem online, and `nmcli con up` activates the connection profile.

questions.question: Lab 7 (Bash Conditional & Variable Assignment): Fix the variable assignment and complete the `if` statement that checks whether `/etc/isulad/daemon.json` is a regular file (`-f`) and prints `Configured`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 346 & 356), Bash variable assignments must not have spaces around `=`, `-f` tests for a regular file, and `if` blocks terminate with `fi`.

questions.question: Lab 8 (Bash Loop & Arithmetic): Complete the `for` loop and arithmetic expression to accumulate the sum of odd numbers (`1, 3, 5, ..., 99`) using `seq` or brace expansion and `$(( ... ))`.
questions.starter_code:
#!/bin/bash
sum=0
for i in $(seq 1 2 99); ____
    sum=____
done
echo $sum
questions.solution:
#!/bin/bash
sum=0
for i in $(seq 1 2 99); do
    sum=$((sum + i))
done
echo $sum
questions.answer: for i in $(seq 1 2 99); do sum=$((sum + i)); done
questions.explanation: Per Ch.06 (pp. 349 & 361), `for ...; do ... done` iterates over the list and `$((sum + i))` performs integer arithmetic expansion.

questions.question: Lab 9 (iSula Container Deployment with Persistent Storage): Write the `isula` command to run an interactive container named `web01` from image `openeuler/nginx:latest`, bind-mounting `/root/html` to `/usr/share/nginx/html` in read-write mode and executing `/bin/bash`.
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp. 407–426), `isula run` creates and starts a container, `-n` specifies the container name, and `-v host:container:rw` mounts persistent storage.

questions.question: Lab 10 (iSula Debugging & Image Cleanup): Write two commands: (1) execute `ip addr` inside a running container named `web01`, and (2) remove an unused local container image `busybox:test`.
questions.starter_code:
isula ____ web01 ip addr
isula ____ busybox:test
questions.solution:
isula exec web01 ip addr
isula rmi busybox:test
questions.answer:
isula exec web01 ip addr
isula rmi busybox:test
questions.explanation: Per Ch.07 (pp. 412 & 438), `isula exec` runs a command inside an active container and `isula rmi` removes a local container image.
